review_text: My wife and did the 3-hour horseback riding with them on December 23, and it was one of the best days of our trip to Patagonia. We stumbled upon the tour by accident, booking the 'Cabalgata Lago Sofia' tour through our hostel, and WOW it did not disappoint! It is about 25m outside of town, so we had to pay extra for transportation there and back. Once there, our guide Zdanke (sp?) took time to make us feel safe and comfortable on the horses. I have gone horseback riding maybe 2 times before, and those 2 times we just walked in a line. This was different: we were briefly trained how to get our horses to walk, trot, turn, stop, etc. Our guide had impeccable English, took the time to make us feel comfortable, and literally DRAGGED me and my horse up the hill when my horse felt a bit stubborn and didn't want to walk with the rest of the group. I'll admit, I got frustrated a couple times, not knowing how to make my horse keep up. But our guide stuck with me, gave me tips, and finally - FINALLY! - I got my horse to walk, trot, and even canter at the end. The scenery is breathtaking. Sign up for the 3 hour tour to get a stunning view over the lake and surroundings. Cost was about 50,000p each (if I remember right - could be off a bit). review_text: I spent three weeks in Chile with a group of college students. I contacted Cristian at Ecotours only to plan a 5 day trek in Torres del Paine national park. After talking with him via email, I wound up planning the rest of our trip through Ecotours, and couldn't be happier. We did tours of Santiago and Valparaiso, as well as 3 days in the Atacama desert and the 5 days in Torres del Paine. Cristian was extremely helpful, never pushy, and very responsive to questions that I had during the process. Each of the guides that he contracted for our tours were excellent. Mauricio led us around Santiago and Valparaiso, and kept the students entertained. In the Atacama desert, Gustavo led our group for 3 days, from the mountains around San Pedro, Valle de la Luna, the altiplano salt lakes, to the top of the Lascar Volcano. Daniel, Ecoutours´ operations manager, went out of his way to help us out during our time in San Pedro. Our driver in San Pedro, Don Carlos, was one of the highlights of our trip. My students enjoyed their conversations with him, and when a couple of kids got sick, he helped take excellent care of them. In Patagonia, Tomas and Armando were excellent. They led our group through 75 miles of hiking over 5 days. They shared their knowledge of the area (Tomas grew up just outside the park), as well as prepared all our meals. Everything during the trip exceeded expectations. I wouldn't hesitate to book another trip with Ecotours.

review_text: As you can see we visited in the off season and it was cold, wet and raining. However we loved the visit. We drove from Pucon and took the first small road off the main road to the area. Hmm not the best road we have travelled but a bit of fun. Single lane, a lot of potholes but through some pleasant countryside. We drove for about 8 kms before coming across the entrance to the falls. Found out straight away we could go back to Pucon the other route. Yippee. Nice elderly couple greeted us to take our $1000 each entrance fee. Parked about 50m from the falls. Fantastic timber walkways surround the falls giving you interesting viewing and places for taking photos. It rained the whole time while we were there but this did not take anything away from the views. Funny way back to the main road was shorter but more pot holes so be ready to take it slow.

review_text: My wife & I recently toured around South America and one of our favourite places was Valparaiso, Chile. We flew into Santiago from Australia and only had 2 days accommodation booked here until we were move on to our next destination, Cusco, Peru. Our travel agent had booked us into a Santiago city tour for our second day, however quite a number of people advised us not to miss going to Valparaiso if we were in Chile. So, we asked our local tour guide who picked us up from the airport if we could change our city tour for the Valparaiso tour, which they did without a problem. Well, were we glad we changed our itinerary! Valparaiso is this funky, arty, colourful town built on the side of the coastal mountains, with thousands of different coloured houses clinging to the sides. To take a walk up and down these vibrant steep streets is just amazing. This places oozes personality, creativeness and charm. If you're dropping into Santiago (most flights from & to Australia land here), make the effort to take the 90 minute trip out to the coast and check it out, it's fantastic!!!

review_text: Booked 3 different private tours with South Excursions while our cruise ship was in Brazil. We had dealt with them in the past in Argentina. We had an agreement to pay cash in US$ at the end of each tour. For that, I had to provide them with my credit card number. Just before our first tour, Stephanie sent me an E.Mail to inform me that her boss had change his mind and that we had to pay in advance with my credit card. This was applied for the first two tours in Maceio and Ilheus. They overcharged me because of the exchange rate and I had to contact them many times before they finally accepted to refund me for the overcharge. This was done more than one month after the tour. As for the tours: In Maceio, we were supposed to embark on a schooner to see the Mundau Lagoons and Islands with a stop at a beach. We were 8 persons from our ship and were looking forward to do this tour. The day before our arrival, South Excursions sent me an Email to inform me that they had a problem with the schooner and that the tour was cancelled. To replace it, they offered an alternative tour for a 2 hours stay at the Praia de Frances beach and a stop at a Craft Market for a lower price. We were very disappointed to be notified so late and I had to contact the other participants on the ship to change our planning for the next day. For this new tour, we had a guide that spoke only Portuguese. With her, they had provided us with a translator. We were in a very comfortable mini-van and the tour was completed in 4 hours before returning to our ship. We had reserved tours in other cities with South Excursions before and never had this kind of problems. In Ilheus, we were 8 persons in a mini-van for a 4 hours tour to visit the city and spend some time at the Millionnaire’s beach. Our guide was 20 years old with limited experience and spoke basic English. He tried his best and we saw all the sites that were included in our program. We had a few stops to taste different drinks prepared with chocolate. For the beach stop, we were taken to a restaurant in front of the Millionnaire’s beach and they provided us with plastic chairs and a parasol. The waves were high and it was a bit difficult to go in the water because of the current. They had free WIFI with very good reception. The tourist industry is not very developed in Ilheus and it was an opportunity to see the main sites in the city with a stop at the beach. Price was too high for what we had for the excursion. In Vitoria, we were 12 persons in a mini-van for a 4 hours tour to visit the city. For this tour, we paid only the day of the tour but I had to give them my credit card number in case of no show. The company that represented South Excursions was Van Vitoria. We had a guide-driver that spoke only Portuguese and another guide that translated in good English. They were both very generous and took us to all the attractions scheduled. They also added many other sites to visit because they wanted to show us as much as possible. We were supposed to have a 4 hours tour and it lasted for more than 6 hours for the same price. We were extremely satisfied with this tour. This was, by far, the best tour we had with South Excursions for Brazil.

review_text: Puerto Montt - Puerto Natales. The food was definitely decent - not as bad as some of the reviews say. I left every meal full and satisfied. The weather was decent and we saw penguins and dolphins. Beautiful. The only thing that was weird was that you do not get a key for the room so you cannot lock it. I felt a little strange about leaving valuables in the room, but I did and it was fine. Loved the trip though. It was nice to read and walk around the boat and watch the mountains and hills go by. We went in off season and had a 4 person room to the two of us. They let us watch movies in the movie room which was great. Like a movie theater. The only thing that was a downer was that alcohol was not allowed at all on the boat. Boo. Also we were dirtbagging around South America and this was a little expensive for us, but still a great experience.

review_text: Loved our stop here to explore this tourist market for about an hour. Some small vendor stalls are located outside and others are inside the inside the market building. Their is really something for just about everyone. We purchased several handicraft item here that were unique. BOTTOM LINE: Well worth you time to visit this market for low cost handmade jewelry, alpaca hats, scarfs and clothing plus rock hound stones, t-shirts, jams, fruits, etc. On the second level are some additional shops and hair salons. The restrooms are upstairs for a nominal fee. The traditional magnets and other tourist souvenirs items can all be found here. MY RATING: 8/10. NEXT DOOR is a fully blown USA style grocery store with loads of things tourist will appreciate. It was great to see a nice selection of USA branded snacks and sodas. We saw many of our fellow cruisers here stocking up, too. I paid with Chilean Pesos but not sure if they also accepted credit cards or USD.

review_text: Our family went just a few days ago to this planetario. It is very well organized and very friendly. We started watching a very instructive 3D movie which explains how a star is born. Our guide Hugo commented all along so it was super interesting and entertaining. Hugo is delightful and keeps everybody engaged in the understanding of our galaxy. Our 8 year old kept asking questions and he would take time to answer him. Then the most amazing is the time Hugo took to show us lots of stars, clusters of stars, and educate us on the constellations of the South Hemisphere. We were only 6 people and each of us took turn, we enjoyed especially the opportunity of having so much time with a telescope. It is really worth a visit, and it is not expensive, 10,000 pesos for adult and half price for kids. We liked the familial ambiance, and the owners serve a nice snack of specialties with a local drink. Watching the stars in the middle of the vineyards has its charm! We went to the 11:30 pm show.

review_text: This was the first stop on our great Central Valley wine tour. The relatively cool Casablanca area between Santiago and Valparaiso houses Chile’s most avant-garde wines, such as Casa Marin in the San Antonio Valley. They are producing new styles of Sauvignons and Pinot Noirs. We had a fantastic guide named Diego. We strolled the grounds, saw the winery, then went upstairs and tasted wine with Diego. He was fantastic and explained about why wines are to be stored on their sides so their corks don’t dry, shrink, and allow air in and evaporate wine out. I must have turned pale because my husband told him I was panicking to get home and put our few nice bottles on their sides! Dear Sarah, It's pleasant to read that you enjoyed our wines and the Casa Marin Experience. We hope to receive you again! Kindly, Hospitality Team.

review_text: Watch out for Taxi scams at Santiago Chile airport. We booked Elife taxi pick up through Booking.com and paid in advance. The taxi never turned up and we had to ask for help from a so called airport assistance person. This is where the scam starts. Everything is in Spanish obviously and he purports to call the taxi firm to find out where the driver is. He tells us the taxi has broken down and you will have to wait about 2 hours for the driver to turn up. He tells you that the alternative is to take a waiting taxi for $30 dollars and Elife will refund you. You decide to go with this and he takes you to a waiting taxi. You arrive at the hotel and the driver wants paying by card. You use his card machine and He tells you your card isn't working so you try another card. In the meantime he has scammed you out of your well earned money by about £2000. Beware of this scam and pay cash

review_text: Visiting Santiago de Chile was a great experience , we went there on September 16 -24-23, In these days Chile commemorate their independence and it takes three days Or sometimes takes one week. there are a lot of activities around the city like the chilean day at the Parque O'Higgins, where you enjoy Chilean rodeo, groups dancing la cueca the official dance from Chile, I also enjoyed drinks like chicha, pisco sour is very good, food like empanadas, barbecue that is excellent and good flavor ect.. Also, the cathedral, the government building are closed but you can enjoy the beautiful architecture, on September 19, there is Army parade, at the Palace of La Moneda there is a presentation of the traditional dance la cueca Tips: If you visit Chile on these Independent dates be aware that all malls, restaurants and stores are close. The PDI Immigration paper keep it like your ID because you have to show it at the hotel. Always carry an extra sweater because sometimes gets very cloudy and cold due to the Andes mountain. specially after 3pm. The best neighborhood to stay is Vitacura. I recommend Hilton Hotel its near de mall, train station, the observatory building and restaurants. Review of: Discover Santiago Half Day Guided Tour Included Local Snack

review_text: Great day, picked up 0900 in la uxe SUV, only me and my colleague, by our guide Marco and the driver/guide Ariel. First an hour drive to Vina de Mar, where we stopped at viewpoint and then headed for the beach area which had a nice Miami Beach style boulevard plus a pier. Then the highlight for me: Fishmarket Valparaiso where pellicans and seelions where at 4 m distance playing in the surf, and waiting for left over fish. After that drive through Valparaiso with viewpoint stops. Nice restaurant, excellent seafood lunch during one hour, nice view, affordable price, advised and booked at our request around 1PM. The guide lives in the city so could tell all details. Special was the inner city, with colourful murals (like you have in Miami), but really nicely done. A pity we could not stay for the evening, since we heard the bars have live music (guitar, salsa, waltzes etc) spontaneously every evening, We left at 1500 towards the winery. It was winter, so no green trees or grapes, we saw the cellars and tasted two wines. That was a bit meager and definitely not the 'show' you get in other countries..Over all a great day. review_text: Since I live in Chile and work in the tourism industry, I did extensive research before deciding how and when to go to Laguna San Rafael and its glaciar. Instead of taking the expensive Skorpios cruise or other companies like Navimag that start in Puerto Chacabuco, we decided to take the new, shorter route from Bahia Exploradores. It is much cheaper (about USD300 per person, including transportation from your hotel in Puerto Rio Tranquilo) and allows you to get to the glaciar in 3 hours only, so if you are short of time, you can do the excursion in just one day instead of 2 days minimum with the others (although taking a two-day tour and sleeping in the forest near the glaciar allows to see more things). It is worth it. As of now, there are only two companies offering excursions from there: Emtrex and Destino Patagonia. All the others sites you will find offering excursions from Bahia Exploradores go through them -and can be more expensive. We went with Destino Patagonia, as they were the first ones to answer my emails (quick email response is important to me) and were friendly and helpful in their reply. Enough of introduction, let's go to the thick of it. Destino Patagonia's driver picks us up at our hotel at Puerto Rio Tranquilo (the closest town from Bahia Exploradores) at 7am, then drives us to Valley Exploradores with his SUV. The road is quite bumpy and I'm glad I'm not driving, so that I can enjoy the stunning landscape around us, with lakes, numerous waterfalls, impressive mountains and glaciars. At 9am, we cross the Exploradores river in a boat (they still need to build a bridge there) and we continue on another van for a minutes on the other side. We finally make it to the pier and get into a tiny boat, where only 6 clients + 2 pilots and our guide can fit in the small cabin. Don't expect comfort: as I wrote before, this is a more adventurous route, and it's better to have waterproof clothes and shoes on. There starts the route to the lagoon San Rafael, which takes about 3 hours. Unfortunately the weather is bad so we cannot get out of the cabin much. It also gets very bumpy at some point because of the waves and strong winds (this is definitely NOT recommended for people with neck or back problems). This is also something worth knowing beforehand: since we are on a tiny boat, there is the possibility that the weather is too bad and we have to return -and you cannot really know it until the boat reaches the fjords (we start from a river). In such cases, 90% of the excursion is refunded. The weather is very cloudy and it rains sporadically, so we cannot really appreciate the beauty of the fjord around us, but once we reach the laguna with all the blue icebergs and the big glaciar, it is spectacular, even with the rain. Because of the bad weather, we cannot picnic on the piece of land next to the glaciar and have to eat inside the boat. The food, however, is unexpectedly good. Then we get close to the big wall of ice and spend about an hour observing it. Amazing beauty, and quite impressive when big pieces of ice dramatically fall on the water. There is a bit of frustration though: first, the guide's English is just ok, and he doesn't give many explanations about the glaciar's formation, the colors, etc. Second, we cannot get as close as the zodiacs coming from Skorpio's and Navimag's boats. These get really to the foot of the glaciar, while our tiny boat cannot. But it is still a great experience. And instead of having the classic drink in a glass with a piece of ice from the glaciar, our guide does something more creative: he picks a big piece of ice, carves a hole in it with his knife, and pours directly the whisky in it. Great idea! As we return, the weather clears up and we can appreciate better the beauty of the area, with the fjords and cascades, and see a couple of penguins and sea lions on the way. Conclusion: This is still a very new route, so there are a few flaws that can be corrected with time and experience (the level of English, the lack of explanations, maybe a better boat that could get close to the glaciar...). But the fast is friendly, it is by far the fastest and cheapest option, and you get actually two excursions in one, as the 2-hour road trip from the village of Puerto Rio Tranquilo to Bahia Exploradores features stunning landscapes, with lakes, numerous waterfalls, impressive mountains and glaciars. Simply one of the most beautiful landscapes in Chile -and I've seen many!

review_text: We had a wonderful day wine tasting with Christian (our tour guide) and Felipe (the driver and an owner of the company). We chose this tour specifically because we were looking for more wine tasting and were not interested in extensive tours of wineries and vineyards. We visited four wineries. Christian told us about each winery and we had one glass of wine at three of the wineries and a flight of three wines at one winery. We started the day at the charming house of a local artist, who prepared breakfast for us. It felt really special to be sharing food in someone’s home rather than at a restaurant. She showed us her art and her husband’s panadería, operated out of a small building on the property. Lunch felt similarly special as we visited another home. The family there runs a B&B in the back and we had an excellent meal prepared by the matriarch. It included asparagus soup, lasagna, and preserved fruit from their property. The real highlight of the day was Christian, our guide, who was a wealth of knowledge about Chile and Chilean culture. He wears many hats: video game storyteller, sommelier, winery tour guide (at a winery in addition to this tour). He has also worked making wine and has an extensive interest and knowledge of Chilean history. I felt that we learned so much, not only about Chilean wine and winemaking, but also about the history and culture of Chile. If we are lucky enough to come back to Chile, we will definitely reserve another tour with Maipo Valley Wine Tours! review_text: The Cementerio General is a truly amazing place to wander, learn more about Santiago's history, and appreciate the somewhat unique way Chileans celebrate and honor their dead. Although it might sound morbid to spend the afternoon wandering through a cemetery, Cementerio General is far more than than that. One can view how families memorialize their family members, how wealthy families for the past 100 years have built massive mausoleums in all kinds of architectural styles, find memorials to military and government leaders, as well as large mausoleums built to honor groups of professionals like the police force, military members, even clowns. Plan to spend a while wandering in the peace and quiet.

review_text: We parked up just before the ranger station in the middle sector - sector Quetrupllian. You can drive on further but only in a truck or land-rover, we couldn't pass even in a utility vehicle as the track is so bad. So we hiked the first 4km on the track through the woods, which is pretty steep in places, before we entered the trail proper to the glacier, which is another 4km. This is the best part of the hike, of course. Wooded with lots of monkey puzzle trees to start with, then opens out on the lava field, with streams, mini waterfalls and rock strata, which you walk through to the glacier and a tremendous view of the volcano. It's the other side that you see from Pucon and more snow covered. Total return journey was four hours, plus stops for lunch and photos. Got great shots of a juvenile condor and red headed woodpecker. Very worthwhile hike.

I actually hiked through the park from the Olmue side.

Could have easily spent another couple hours biking (or alternatively had lunch), was back at the hotel in Santiago by 14:00 hrs.

review_text: Chiloe, once one gets past Ancud, is a beautiful, otherworldly island, with rolling hills, fields, and an all-pervasive sense of peace. We visited the pinguinieras as a day-trip from Puerto Varas (eminently doable; the ferry-service to Chiloe is outstanding, and even boasts clean bathrooms and Wi-Fi!!). The Pinguinieras are located on an outstandingly scenic back road high up the Pacific, finally leading down to a beach, with the penguin islands visible close offshore. The Pacific was *very* stormy when we went (the police had actually forbidden the boats all day from going out, and ours was only the second one out), which just added to the enjoyment- not for those who get easily seasick, however; this water is choppy. It was unbelievable how close we were able to get to the penguins- and there were dozens of them. This whole Chiloe trip was just beautiful.

review_text: We hired PrivateTours.cl to take four of us on an 11 hour tour from our cruise ship docked at San Antonio, Chile to the Santiago airport. We worked by email with Esteban. He was very helpful and always responded promptly. We specified in advance that we liked nature and did not want to see any more churches, museums, or go shopping. Our driver, Filipe, and guide, Ben, arrived with an immaculate Mercedes van and we headed up into the Andes. Ben provided interesting narration when appropriate and answered our questions. He was knowledgeable and funny. We made a mid-morning snack stop at a quaint restaurant in a small town. Good fun and excellent food. Then we continued into the mountains. Filipe was an excellent driver, especially important on the narrow, unpaved mountain roads with no guard rails. We stopped at a beautiful mountain lake where Ben set up a table and chairs and served an excellent lunch including a terrific Chilean wine. Then we went back to Santiago to a park with great panoramic views of the city where half the population of Chile lives. Then a cable car ride down to where Filipe was waiting to take us to the airport, right on time. A wonderful day!

review_text: We had an enjoyable visit to this small winery on the outskirts of Santiago. We chose to come here specifically because we had not heard of the winery before in our own country. We reached it using the Metropolitano and then by taxi. Initially our taxi driver couldn't locate the winery (he wanted to take us to the much larger Vina Cousino Macul winery nearby), but we eventually found it: on one side new housing estates, on the other hills rising all the way up to the spectacular snow-capped Andes. This is a small winery founded by several Frenchmen from Aquitaine - hence the name. Wine is produced using traditional artisan techniques. We were given a very well presented tour and explanation, followed by some wine tasting (we were surprised at how much we were charged, and that we had to book our tour/tasting beforehand - but understand that this is normal practice in Chile).

review_text: My partner and I saw a flyer of « BirdsChile », and when we read about their aims on their website, we were convinced that this organisation could be the right for us, as we like nature very much and as we are looking for a tourism respecting and protecting nature as much as possible. As we slept there on a camping for two nights, there was a lot of stuff to organise, which was done perfectly well. To bring us to the starting points of the trekking and to bring us back to our hotel afterwards, we had a car with a conductor who made us feel very safe on any kind of road. The guides Marcela and Felipe were just great; they liked to explain and discuss with us about nature and about Chile; they shared their knowledge and passion for nature with us and gave us the opportunity to get close to the amazing birds, plants and nature around us. They took care of all our needs and wishes so that we felt very comfortable even when the trekking became challenging for us. That’s why we can only warmly recommend « BirdsChile » because the people behind do their job with big empathy and professionalism.

review_text: We engaged Chile Dream Tours for a full day private excursion to Viña del Mar and Valparaiso from Santiago. It was a 5 STAR experience. Our tour guide, Sean Casey, was excellent, a wonderful guide, informative, funny, and extremely attentive to our requests and discussed all manor of questions we had about life in 2022 Chile. Sean lived in the US for 18 year and is fully bi-lingual with near flawless English and Spanish. After the fact we learned that he is also the Operations Manager for the company. We were kept informed both before and after the tour via Whats App. The SUV was clean and comfortable for the 9-hour excursion. At every stop and throughout the day Sean took many photos of our group, which he sent us via e-mail. These are among the best photos of our time in Chile. On the drive from Santiago to our first stop in Viña del Mar we were regaled with the history of Chile from its founding by the Spanish. The drive from Santiago to the first stop in Viña del Mar was an ever-changing landscape from a major city to vineyard and farmlands to the first sighting of the Pacific Ocean and finally the views from the cliffs overlooking this seaside resort city. This tour of Valparaíso was the highlight of the cities we visited in Chile due Sean’s marvelous narrative skills and local knowledge. After a drive through the city we began the walking tour in the city center and boarded the Funicular Reina Victoria, for the ride to the upper half of Valparaiso. review_text: Wandering the streets of San Pedro, you'll come across at least 50 different tour companies. I stumbled into Vive Atacama after only having an hour of sleep in the previous 36 hours, not knowing that this action would be one of the defining ones of my trip. Claudio had a positive energy, explaining the tours they offer and asking me how long I was in town and then expertly recommending the tours I could take. He was inviting and sincere, not for one minute while I was in the agency did I feel like he was trying to sell me a package; it felt more like a friend who was sharing. I ended up booking 5 tours for the 4 days I was there and the cost averaged to about 20 luca (20.000CLP) and all included at least one food - breakfast (coffee/tea/juice or chocolate milk, bread, cheese, marmalade, ham and cookies), lunch (self serve tuna fajita wraps), snack (pisco sours, cookies, chips) but not the entrance fees for the parks (ranged between 2 and 18 luca). Tours booked: Valle de la luna (afternoon/evening), Salar de Tara (full day with two meals), Lagunas Altiplanicas (morning), Laguna Cejar (afternoon/evening), Geysers del Tatio (morning). Claudio did a wonderful job of explaining what I needed to bring with me to be prepared for my tours. I would recommend good, comfortable shoes (I had combat type boots that were probably not the best, but it was either that or sneakers and I felt more comfortable with my ankle covered - especially since I don't like sand and dirt inside my shoes - the most 'hiking' was on the Valle de la Luna tour), for the early morining and evening tours, make sure that you wear layers and for Salar de Tara, bring something to cover your head. It's extremely windy (and we were there on a 'nice day') so keep that in mind. Bring at least 1-2liters of water, and drink it! Bring a towel and a swimsuit for the hot springs and the Geysers and Laguna Cejar. The morning tours there is a van that picks you up from your hotel/hostel and then drops you off in the center of town. Yes, the "star" of the trip was the indescribably breathtaking landscape and nature that Atacama has to offer (volcanos, desert, lagunas, geisers, salt flats, salt caves, flamigos, llamas, vicunas, fox...the list goes on). However, I don't know that I would have appreciated it as much as I did without the guides from Vive Atacama. They were knowledgable and passionate, open to any questions and able to draw from technical answers to local legends and cultural history. Macarena, Roberto and Francisco (the driver for 3 of my tours) were superb. They knew me by name and engaged in personal conversations - asking what I'd done and seen since I last saw them, asking what I was planning on doing next, giving recommendations of where to visit in Chile. As a solo traveler on tours with a majority of pairs or small groups, this truely made an impact. It was also comforting to know that Macarena was trained to administer medical aid, especially when you're at 4.500m (around 15,000 ft) in the middle of the desert. I do speak Spanish and there was only one or two tours where people needed the English translation, and all I can say is that so much of the richness gets lost in translation. There is so much information to share that once you've said it in one language, it's difficult to remember and repeat all the same information in the second. Thank you very much Carla for your opinion, we are glad for your nice experience with us ,we realize you enjoy a lot here, and we hope you recomend with your friends our services. Best Regards!

It was not that long ago, and many Chileans alive today remember all too well. The power in the museum is in the individual stories of what people endured and how they struggling successfully to overthrow the military dictatorship. Nixon's government supported the coup, and therefore the US does bear some responsibility, but this connection is little emphasized in the exhibitions, which include many short films made at the time of the coup and after, as well as artefacts. Ideally, one might visit this museum and Pablo Neruda's house in Santiago the same day, as it was partically destroyed in the coup - out of pure maliciousness, as the Nobel Prize winner was over 70, quite ill, and not even living there at the time. It has been beautifully restored, and your spirits will be restored by a visit there after the seeing Museum of Memory and Human Rights.

review_text: We arranged for the visit to Mamalluca as part of a three-day astronomy/outdoors tour of Chile. It was the first night, right after we got into Santiago from the US, connected on LAN to La Serena, and spent the day touring La Serena and Coquimbo - so it was a long day and night for us! Ours was an English-speaking tour (nice perk in a place where few speak English), but it was way too big a group - several families with unruly children, and frankly more than the guide (who was quite competent in terms of stargazing) could really handle given the facilities at the site (just getting everyone into the main observatory to see things was a challenge). The big downside of the large group is very little time on telescope for anyone when 20+ people have to see things. Positives included getting pictures down the scope (the guide was good at this, but with the big group it slowed things down more), and the remarkable clear/dry skies of northern Chile. Overall, glad we did it, but probably I won't seek it out again.

review_text: Our hotel was in front of this hill, and with all the trees and greenery it is a very nice looking park indeed. There is a walk up to the top, which goes by a fort which is closed and ends at the top of the hill, which provides one of three beautiful vantage points overlooking the city (the other two are San Cristobal and Sky Costanera). Really, the natural part of the park is lovely and the view excellent. However, the site could use some more maintenance. The Japanese Garden looks abandoned, without any water in the pools. The sidewalk along the drive isn't very good, and even unsafe in parts. And the final steps up to the top have rather flimsy railings which could cause some insecurity in people who are at all acrophobic. But it certainly is a pleasant place to be and popular with tourists and locals. You have to sign in when you enter.

review_text: Of all the markets in this area of Santiago this was our favorite by far.....Laid back atmosphere, very straightforward. Fruits, vegetables, nuts, sundries and a bit of merchandise downstairs and an AMAZING array of food stalls packed with locals of all walks upstairs. It can seem overwhelming but the food was very good, home made and super affordable. We at Cafeteria Melantojo where we had basically three courses plus a choice of fresh squeezed juice for the equivalent of about $9 USD. First was a thin chicken consommé type soup, the server will ask you which vegetables you want but this is really your chance to build a salad or just have some sliced cucmbers or shredded cabbage or carrots. All fresh, clean and tasty. The salsa type condiments on the table are also VERY good and spicy. A fair amount of the produce downstairs is for canning or pickling, so be sure to ask. For instance the small yellow papayas are NOT sweet and all the cherries were pie cherries. Still a super fun afternoon in the market and an excellent, funky latin-reggae band playing.

review_text: We booked our tour package via an aggregator over the internet. They subcontracted many of the actual activities through Desert Adventure in San Pedro. We were very happy they did! We took five full tours with them: Valle de la Luna, Lagunas Altiplánicas, Tour Laguna Cejar, Valle Arcoiris, and the Tour Astronómico. All were outstanding, and they did everything they could to make it more than just "sightseeing:" the tours were informative, educational, and memorable. Rather than discuss the specific tours, I'd rather talk about how the guides were very responsive to our interests and very solicitous of our group in particular (we had the oldest customer they'd ever had, a 91-year-old who couldn't do the longer hikes).On most tours, the guides were bi-lingual, and gave the information first in Spanish then in English, but on some tours they sent a separate guide to who spoke English to us. It wasn't just the guides, either. The drivers they work with were very helpful getting in and out of the vehicle, volunteering to take pictures of us at some of the lookouts, and on some occasions pointing out wildlife. I paid 4000 pesos to enter the park, if you want you can skip the entre by entering the street near the restaurant, afterworts you go left and follow the signs. Youre walking thru scenic routes, you'll see lakes, snow, animals. When your at the top of the mountain, 1550 meter. You will start at 1240 meter. At the top you have a scenery of five volcanos including the vilarica. Going down will take you 2-3 hours. And the bus back is 30 minutes.

review_text: My friend and I signed up online for a tour of the Santiago Cemetery and the Bellavista neighborhood where we were staying. Esteban was the booking agent. He made it very easy for us to schedule a time that fit our needs and make payment online. We then decide we also wanted to take a tour of Isla Negra the next day. Jeanette (tour guide) and Felipe (driver) picked us up at our apartment right on time and gave us a tour of the cemetery. She knew so much history about the people buried there and their roles in Chilean politics. We spent a couple of hours there, but unfortunately my friend wasn't feeling well. We asked if after our neighborhood tour they could drop us off at a clinic our apartment manager told us about. Jeanette said she couldn't just leave us there and proceeded to take us in to translate, sat with us while we waited for the next couple of hours, and interpreted what the doctor said. She then took us to the pharmacy to get some preliminary medicine. All this time Felipe was patiently waiting in our van. The next day we had Jeanette and Felipe on a tour to Isla Negra where one of the homes of Chilean poet Pablo Neruda was right on the beach. It has been turned into a museum and we had a wonderful lunch there. Afterward we visited the town of Pomaire known for its earthenware pottery. When we got back into Santiago, Felipe and Jeanette took us back to the clinic so my friend could get her second medication. I felt that we were in such good hands with Private Tours Santiago. Jeanette had called Esteban when my friend got sick, and he said staying with us was the right thing to do. I feel like I made some new friends in Santiago and will choose them again if I go back. Thanks so much!

review_text: I did the Aysen Glacier Trail in Feb 2012 and it was one of the best physical/spiritual experiences i have ever had. The area is stunningly beautiful and the folks at PAEX are truly the nicest people i have ever met. If you are looking for an educational environmental trip that is physically demanding and takes you deep into a place where few humans have been to - this is the trip for you. You need to be in reasonable shape - you will be on your feet for 10 hours a day. Some Advice: Get the right equipment and pack light. If you are thinking about hiring a porter, you are carrying too much stuff. Less is more. Here is the basic equipment you need: 1) backpack/snowpack (waterproof is good - you will encounter rain) 2) 2 trekking pants - one for camp, one for trekking 3) 1 base layer 4) 1 mid layer (fleece jacket) 5) 1 waterproof shell (top and bottom) 6) Gaiters (very important - you dont want your hiking boots to be soaked and you will walk in water) 7) Trekking poles (again very very important - this is the first time i used trekking poles and it saved my knees) Also definitely get to Balmaceda one day early - do not take the risk of missing your flight and having one day less to do the trek.

Metal working, ceramics and jewelry were also on display.

It is not cheap, but we all agreed that it was worth it.

review_text: We completed the W Trek at the start of May. This review is not about advice on which route to take but more about what you need and what to expect. In saying that we caught the last Catamaran to Paine Grande and from there headed north to Lago Grey and then continued west to east. We were lucky as we could stay in some refugio's and use their facilities for a fee. We hired most of our gear and while most of it operated well it was the mattresses and sleeping bags that let us down. Not ideal when it's below zero during the nights. We discussed with most other travellers and we all agreed it was irresponsible for the agencies to hire out gear in it's condition. Not sure if it's overuse, lack of care, wrong maintenance and cleaning or a mixture of both but our sleeping bags (rated to extreme -12 centigrade) failed to keep us warm and we spent most night shivering and no sleep. Our floor mats were pretty useless as well. If we were to do the trek again we would invest in the compact inflatable mattresses and a high grade sleeping bag. You can always try sell it in Puerto Natales to other travellers. You will loose some money but the nights in the park will be worth it. Other tings that could be useful on the trip; Self rolling compression bags for you warm gear and change of clothes (they usually protect from the water as well) A days extra food Walking poles - we found them perfect for the trip as they helped us on all occasions. They took a few hours to get used to but after a few hours we could set a good pace with the poles. Plastic bags for use in your bag (bag covers can be hard in the wind) Thermos for tea and coffee - helps if you want to eat on the go. Heat Patches - in the sleeping bag or jacket at night Apart from that hiking in May was amazing. WE had clear days with not a cloud in the sky and not a single wisp of wind. The national park fee was cheaper and we didn't have to pay at all the camps. Also most of the streams are frozen over making it easy to cross without removing our shoes.

review_text: Just spent a few days in Atacama Desert... booked 3 days of excursions through Grad10 before leaving the UK. The excursions were genuinely exceptional. review_text: We learned a lot about grapes at this vineyard. For instance, they talked about the 242 grape like it was something everyone knew. When I asked my other wine tasting companions if they had ever heard of it, they all said no. The 242 is actually a Sauvignon Blanc grape clone that came from France. The 242 is characterized by grapes on small clusters and an early ripening period. It produces wines with a vibrant stone fruit character, marked mineral notes and lashings of spice and citrus fruits. Also, it conveys the mineral/salty character which comes from the 110-million-year-old decomposed granite soils.

review_text: The giant Moai is in front of the Fonck Museum. It has a more officla title which is the Museo de Arqueología e Historia Francisco Fonck. So who is Mr. Fonck? He was a Prussian anthropologist who was quite a collector. He lived between 1830 and 1912. The first thing you see from the outside is the giant Moai which you might recognize from Easter Island. Inside, the Fonck has an excellent exhibit on the history of Chile that is infused with plenty of art by the indigenous people of South America including the Rapa Nui from Easter Island. I didn't think this was going to be very interesting but I was wrong - the museum was fascinating and we learned a lot.

review_text: Vina Maquis is a vineyard leading in and recognized for its environmental sustainability practices. While dedicated to the environment, the vineyard has a decidedly modern edge to it. Uniquely situated between two rivers, the vineyard is both expansive and selective as to the grapes used in its wines. All wines are produced in the on site facility that is wrapped by an open louvred building covered in climbing vines for temperature modulation. A geothermal exchange plant powers all of the energy needs of the vineyard and winery, reducing Maquis’ carbon footprint by 90%. Pablo was our gracious host and wonderful sommelier. Pablo speaks English beautifully. He is passionate about wine, especially Maquis. He shared 5 EXQUISITE wines with us, including many with a Cab Franc component. Cab Franc is one of our favorite grapes and both the blends (Lien, especially) and Maquis Franco (100%) were out of this world delicious. They were also a nice contrast the more typical red wines produced in the Colchagua valley. Maquis is comfortable playing with and adjusting its blends annually, depending on the characteristics and environmental variations of the yield from year to year. The wines can be enjoyed early, as well as aged for up to 20+ years. These wines were a revelation. Maquis is cutting edge in an industry steeped in traditional practices. They have bottled an incredible recipe for kind earth practices and creative wine making to terrific result. A visit to Maquis is a special stop to include while enjoying the Colchagua valley. We deeply thank you for your comments, which reflects extraordinary well all the full concept we have in Maquis, based on sustainability, respect of the environment and quality wines. We will congratulate Pablo for his great work. Hope to see you again in our winery. Best regards from Viña Maquis, at the Colchagua Valley

review_text: This was our first excursion on arrival into San Pedro de Atacama and I think probably wise to do it before others as the comparisons to other destinations would make it feel less impressive. We chose to travel with Whipala Expeditions but virtually all tour agencies run this very popular tour. The tour commenced at 4pm (although the bus was 10 minutes late) and we met at the agency. We were back at 7.30pm though the advertised time is 8pm. It is one of the cheaper tours of all the tours. We had a small group of 12, which is a good number and our guide Bruce, spoke excellent English and was very knowledgeable of the area. The Valle de la Luna is just a short drive from San Pedro and involved 3 stops for walking before the final stop to watch the sunset. We visited the Salt Caves, taking about 40 minutes to walk through quite small spaces and sometimes in darkness (use your torch on your phone). If you are not very mobile or get a bit claustrophobic, this bit would be difficult, especially as you are there with about 15 other tour groups all taking it in turns. After this, a short drive to the Grande Dunas, which is a rather spectacular sand dune amongst a real lunar style landscape. This is about a 45 minute walk and you can take your time or go a bit further according to your desire. Back in the bus and onwards to The Three Marias, which is a fairly unimpressive outcrop of 3 rocks (in fact one of them has broken) - a two minute stop before jumping back in the bus for 30 minutes to take us to Coyote Rock where we stay to watch the sunset. This is fairly scary to watch many people walking so close to the cliff edge to get the best photo. If you are afraid of heights (as I am), don’t go too close to the edge! However, watching the changing colours on the landscape in the valley below is quite stunning. The most stunning colours occur before the sun actually sets and then once the sun is below the horizon, it is another 30 minutes before the sky changes to the really stunning colours, but we are well and truly in the bus on the way back before we get to see this. If you are reasonably fit, you could do hire bikes and do this tour under your own steam. You would definitely need a light to get back though. If you take any of the tours (and it didn’t look like there was a huge amount of difference between them), then make sure you wear good walking shoes, bring at least a litre of water and something warm to wear for the last part as when the wind picks up, the temperature is quite cold. Also sunglasses and sunscreen and perhaps a light snack.

review_text: There are three main areas, stretching around a kilometre along the bottom of a valley that has plentiful bird life and numerous small rodents (chinchillas?) running around among the varied vegetation – cacti and aromatic bushes, with some larger trees where the stream ran through the valley bottom. The rock carvings themselves were a little underwhelming; many were hard so see in the sunlight, and lacked the wow factor that I had perhaps hoped for. Maybe I was hoping for obviously spaceship-like carvings in the fashion of Erich von Daniken. Nonetheless there were a large number, as well as a lesser number of painted ones (again very indistinct). The area beyond the picnic area at the Western end is possibly the best, with one rock in particular covered with several primitive stick figure carvings and lusher vegetation including willow. It's easy to reach by car from Ovalle - just take the main road towards the coast and Santiago (which is not signed, of course in Ovalle itself), and after a few kilometres turn left onto an unmade road following the signpost. Although you can park at the barrier, most people seem to take their cars into the valley proper - in June (winter) it was very quiet and peaceful.

It is also part of the End of the World Route, a scenic touristic route. Certainly would very highly recommend visiting Cueva Del Milodon to any tourist in Puerto Natales or Punta Arenas.

It's definitevely a MUST!

review_text: Pablo Neruda is renowned for his poetry. One of two Nobel Laureates in Literature (the other being his teacher Gabriela Mistral), he is a beloved figure throughout Chile. But Mr. Neruda's creativity was by no means limited to his way with words. Evidence of that is La Chascona, his Santiago home, constructed high in the hills above Chile's capital. "Chascona" refers to the wild hair of Neruda's lover/third wife, and the house is built with a similar carefree approach, expanding from one level up into the hill where it is situated. The decor displays Neruda's love of the sea and of collecting unique and unusual items. And his love of La Chascona (the woman who inspired the house). There's a guided audio tour that is worth getting, as it provides background and stories that enhance the overall experience. Available in English and Spanish (and possibly other languages). The explanations for each section were about the same length; my friend (from Santiago) and I went through together and nearly always finished listening at the same time. If one had to wait longer, there was plenty of interest to occupy our attention. The museum is near some great restaurants in short walking distance, as well as Cerro de San Cristobal and its associated park land and zoo (plus funicular that takes you to the top).

review_text: Don't be fooled, this is a tourist trap. Your "tour" starts with 30 other people in a bus, you'll be driven about 10 minutes out of town where there are several other groups doing the exact same "tour" thing and then it will dawn on you, you're caught in a somewhat expensive tourist trap. The busses just drive around you with headlights on bringing new groups into rotation. You will have to stand up for the first 60 minutes while someone with a laser points out stars and the zodiac signs. Yes, that is 60 minutes standing up watching the stars while there are busses with headlights driving around. At one point we could not hear the guy with the laserpointer anymore due to the engine noise around us. Next part of the tour are the telescopes. You will be lucky if you have a few minutes of actual viewing time as the celestial objects obviously constantly go out of view and they have to re-adjust them and everybody is basically just cueing up to have a peek. After that you get a cup of warm chocolate milk and some more talking but inside, as other groups move in on the telescopes. 2 star tour, would not recommend. Review of: Atacama Desert Stargazing Tour

review_text: Very cool and refreshing experience to float on the laguna. Finding up-to-date info online can be difficult so here are some things that we learned: 1. While biking is the most cost-effective way to get there without a car ($8,000 pesos to rent a basic bike), the road there is INCREDIBLY bumpy. The blogs and reviews I read really downplayed this. I cycle daily so I'm used to a bike seat - but I was wincing in pain for most of the ride, about an hour and 15 minutes each way. If you're only an occasional cyclist (like my husband), the pain is excruciating. If you're on the fence about biking vs. booking a tour, book the tour! Your body will thank you. 2. If you still want to visit on your own, you need to buy tickets in advance on their website and select a specific time slot. You can't buy tickets at the park gate. Again with outdated info online - we had no idea about this and thankfully our bike rental guys asked where we planned to go and filled us in! Once at the laguna you have an hour to visit and 30 minutes to float - which sounds super strict but it was a lot more chill than it sounds! Beautiful spot with views of the mountains.

review_text: My husband and I took the Maipo Valley wine tour in mid-April during harvest time. It turned out to be the perfect time to visit the wineries because we got to actually see the grapes on the vines and even taste the different varieties. Tom was our guide and took excellent care of us. Our Spanish is very rough, and he was able to translate everything for us with ease. The tour included a visit to a certified organic wine producer where we touched on organic wine production and had a (very) generous tasting, then on to a micro-winery who is also practicing organic wine production (but not officially certified) where we learned in depth about wine production and had another (very generous) tasting. Our final stop was at the restaurant and shop of another winery where we did an olive oil tasting and had lunch with a blinded wine taste test. Lunch was at extra cost, but reasonably priced and generous portions. Thanks for a great tour!

review_text: We vistied OWM wines (with Jose and Mariela from Casa Pando in Santa Cruz). An easy 15 to 20 minutes from central Santa Cruz, it's located in a tranquil setting in Lolol, up and over the 'cerro' in the next valley. Winemaker José and viticulturist Jaime greeted us. Jaime shared the history about his family's land and farming, and how OWM Wines started. They explained the 2010 earthquake wrecked havoc on their main building. They recently erected a new, sturdier building with a small adobe room in the back (lab and barrel room) to keep a piece of history intact. If ever there was a small, boutique artisan producer, this is it!!! We tasted 2 Petit Sirah, 2 Petit Verdot and Carménère from barrel, each with slightly different approach. For example, utilizing naturally occurring yeast versus adding a standard manufactured yeast creates slightly different aromas and tastes in the wine. The Petit Verdot with natural yeast reminded me of a "wild man", thus our name for this wine during our visit. Afterwards we each got to make a blend choosing what percentage of which wine we wanted to add. We then blind tasted each of the five different blends (José made a blend too) and ranked them from favorite to least favorite. This was an amazing overall experience! We learned a great deal and gained a greater appreciation for what they are doing at OWM. In addition to their wines, they work with clients to produce custom blends. Note this is a small operation, a reservation is necessary for a tour and tasting. Highly recommend a visit. Thanks so much Jaime and José! We look forward to enjoying our OWM Handmade 2 Cepas (and to visiting you again)!

review_text: If we would have ever got a chance to ride in the balloon, I have no doubt it would have been excellent. Booked for 2 people nearly a month before via Civitatis. A few days before departure I was contacted via Whatsapp, asking if we could move to the day before. This I was told was because they require 4 people to fly. We couldn't do a day earlier as we weren't going to be in the Atacama at that time, so we were told hopefully somebody would book in for the following 2 days. We were disappointed as nowhere on the booking did it mention the need for 4 people, but we remained hopeful. The day of our initial booking, I was contacting the company asking if anybody else had booked for the following morning. I sent multiple WhatsApp's, emails and instagram messages, our Airbnb owner even tried ringing for me. All contact was ignored until very late in evening. When we were told nobody else had booked so it could not go ahead Really wanting to do this experience, I wondered if maybe I could pay extra to make sure it happened. I asked if the need for 4 people was due to weight, I told 'yes, it is a minimum of 4'. So I didn't persist with asking if there was a price that would allow us to fly just the 2 of us. The next afternoon, great news! I was invited to a Whatsapp group with 2 other people and the company stating we were finally due to fly the following morning. An hour later I was told the people that had booked that day, wished to fly just the 2 of them and had paid for that privilege! I was obviously very annoyed and shocked this was the outcome. I told the company this was unacceptable and they needed to prioritise my booking, and I would pay for the privilege of flying as a 2. An option I didn't know was available to me. as I was told it had to be 4 people because of weight. They told me this was not possible. Why they decided to take that persons money over mine makes no sense to me. That morning was our last chance to ride as we left the next day. Book but know that you might not be able to ride when you want if at all.

review_text: I hink enough people have described the tour so i will just provide a few tips. We booked through pamela tours and ended up on a grouo with terra extreme. We had an english/spanish guide. Im not sure the guide was necessary because all he did was tell us when we were at the geysers, the thermal springs, when to get a photo, toilets, instructions. There was absolutely no discussion on how geysers are formed, when they were discovered, does the geyser field change, why doesnt it smell, no discussion on vegetation or anything. That was disappointing. I had to ask the guide for more info. So for the tour disappointing but the acyual geyser and thermal spring was great. Also we got to the brekky spot a bit late spending more time with thw geysers to find that people were piling into their 3rd and 4th pieces of food whilst we were lucky to scoff some down ao be careful not to miss out. Wear absolutely every piece of warm clothing you can including a scarf to cover your nose as this will freeze. The spot on the furthest right as you get in the thermal springs is the warmest area. I believe the geysers on the salt flat tour (yet to complete) smell very bad so doing the tatio tour separately was recommended. This is a must do.

review_text: This was a fairly early pick up from my hotel in Providencia, which was great as it helped avoid traffic and got us to our destination in really good time. Our small group was guided by Gabriel and Hector, who were very informative, knowledgeable and, at times, funny in a really nice way. I find it much better when the guides interact with the guests rather than sticking entirely to a script and that happened here much to my delight. On arrival at the lake we we given time to explore on our own and to take photos of the stunning scenery including views of the snow capped mountains (it was February, late summer). review_text: I chose Summit Chile for my Villarrica climb because of positive opinions and seeing the name on various blogs. My first contact with the company was very positive- Suzy was extremely friendly, gave me all the information I needed and clarified doubts. I did the climb with Helder, Etgar and Claudio in a small group. There were other groups climbing at the same time and I could see that our group was taking our time, not hurrying too much. Among other equipment they also provide hiking poles, which the hikers in some other groups didn't have. Claudio was the guide doing most of the talking about the surroundings and I learned new things about the plants, rocks, surrounding lakes and the Mapuches. Very interesting information. Now something about the attitude of the guides. Helder and Etgar were very friendly, giving constructive advice, but I couldn't say the same 100% about Claudio. Of course I could see him talk to other group members in a friendly way, have normal conversations with them, joke and laugh, but for some reason he didn't have the same kindness directed at me. I have to admit that I'd never hiked with an organized group, so it was a bit difficult for me to adjust to the rhythm of the main guide - Helder - and walk slower (I'm a fast walker). Claudio after that explained whe should place our feet exactly where the college in front of us did, then added that we were actually paying for this. Later when we were already on much higher level, he again gave the same advice - could have been my mistake once again, but being 1,65 m and making steps the same size as a much taller male hiker in front of me wasn't a very easy task. While climbing, Claudio cheered up the other hikers, made references to their countries and languages- nothing like this happened in my case. When we were taking a break, I wanted to grab my own hiking poles which were lying on the ground because the wind was quite strong and I wanted to protect them from falling. This for for Claudio was good enough to ask "what are you doing?" with a tone that made it sound as if I were doing something absolutely ridiculous, while I simply wanted to make sure my own private equipment was safe. For questions I made I was receiving very brief answers. Even after the hike, already back in the office, when I asked about something not directly related to the hike, Claudio's expression at the moment of me starting to make the question was just telling me "what the hell do you want?". So yes, we pay for following the steps of the person in front of us, but I think we also pay for having supportive guides. Whether I would recommend this company - yes, I'd still do it, the equipment was good, the guides have experience and know what they're doing - only some more kindness was missing. It's not very nice when we all pay the same amount of money and some get a friendly guide and some not such a very friendly one :(

review_text: Prior to our South Pacific Cruise, we spent two days in Santiago, Chile, where we planned on touring several Chilean wineries. Luck brought us to Chilean Wine Lovers...we needed two nights accommodations, a city tour of Santiago during the first day after our 9:00 am arrival from Houston, a tour of several Chilean wineries on Day 2, and transfer to Valparaiso and our cruise ship on Day 3. Mauricio went above, beyond, and over the top for us. He arranged for us to be met at the airport, followed by a very informative tour of central Santiago including lunch. At 4:00 pm we checked into the beautiful Santiago boutique hotel Mauricio arranged for us -- Le Reve - for two nights. A WONDERFUL place to stay in Santiago! On day 2, following our breakfast at Le Reve, Mauricio picked us up at the front door, and 2.5 hours later we arrived at Lapostolle’s Clos Apalta Winery in the Colchaqua Valley – fantastic tour, fantastic wines, and fantastic time. Then we were off to Via Manent for more touring and a great lunch at their local restaurant on-site. During our day, Mauricio shared his incredible knowledge of the Chilean Wine Industry with stories, histories, and anecdotes that made our day complete – he’s a wine expert! We returned late in the afternoon, tired and exhilarated by the day. Day 3 arrived, and there was Mauricio - waiting to take us to Valparaiso and the port…but before we arrived in Valparaiso he treated us to one more tour in the Casablanca Region at Bodega Wines, where they use clay pots for making wine! We loved the wines we tasted at Bodega – and we highly recommend this wine tour. Finally Mauricio dropped us at the port in Valparaiso where our cruise ship waited. We could not have asked for more from Mauricio – he is a wonderful host, and we feel we’ve made a good friend. If you plan to visit Santiago’s wine regions, become knowledgeable of the Chilean Wine Industry, have several great, great tours, and meet a superb host who will handle all of the details, contact Mauricio at Chilean Wine Lovers. We will return to Chile in the future -- our first call will be to Mauricio. Marvilloso!

review_text: Armed with the address, we found two of the only taxi drivers without gps in the city!! It was a longish trip out (CP10,000) there but then at least the driver that returned to pick us up knew where to go (only CP7,000 on the way home)! We did Ruta 2, it took about 2.5 hours and requires a reasonable amount of stamina to go uphill, in spite of the label 'easy climb'. There is a little cascade at the middle of the walk (where you turn around to come back) which would be a nice place for lunch. We did not hang around though, as there was rain threatening. There is a little climbing frame for the kids near the cafe - which has a good range of reasonably healthy food including trailmix and muesli bars to take on the walk, and more lunch options. It looks like they are constructing a high-ropes course as well - hope to go back and try it out one day.

review_text: A disappointment. Normally all daily tours already include transportation to the venue. I thought it was weird for them to sell the transfer separately from the boat ride, but I trusted. It turns out that this was cancelled due to the bad weather conditions. So Patagonia Planet returns the tour money, but not the transport, since it was done. The information that the tour would depend on climatic conditions was somewhat lost in the middle of a huge text and, moreover, with some ambiguity, since it was not clear that we would not even start the navigation. What was written is that we would approach Grey if the weather allowed. I have verified that they have now updated the text and do not even mention the possibility of suspension. The refund of the tour was made via credit card refund after almost a month of exchange of messages with the operator. After all, it is a typical post-pandemic program: only the user loses money, the operator at least earns something with the transportation.

review_text: This is hands-down one of the best experiences I have ever had. Doing a horse trek through the Atacama desert has been a long-held dream of mine and one of the few I've accomplished where the reality was even better than the expectation. Firstly, the staff are all wonderful. It is run by Sergio and Valerie who look after all the details, from looking after the horses to arranging meals on the trip (the meals were absolutely fabulous! I think Valerie missed her calling as a chef - the use of fresh local ingredients and delicious herbs was incredible, especially in dishes that were delivered to our campsites to be cooked over the fire. I don't know how they did it but those desert meals were some of the best of the entire trip). The guide we had and those we met at the ranch spoke English, and was exceptionally knowledgeable. Our guide knew each of the horses - their quirks, personalities and tendencies - and ensured that they were always looked after, and that we were always warned of difficult terrain, equine behaviours etc that we needed to know. The horses were well looked after, hardy, strong and sound. Their energy was evident and, when I asked the guide about how the horses were cared for, he told me that they were always rested for several days between treks. Any trek longer than 4 days requires a change of horse, as they deem it cruel to go any longer. I also found that the horses were ideally matched to each individual, and they evidently put thought into which horses were compatible to trek together. The Atacama itself is beyond words - utterly stunning and beyond belief gorgeous. Seeing it on horseback was just extraordinary. There are no words to describe it. Again, I can't speak highly enough of Rancho Cactus, the staff, their wonderful horses and the whole operation, which runs utterly flawlessly. I would advise, though, that you take note of the advice on their website about skill levels. The 4 day trek was hard work. My husband and I are both experienced riders, and by the end, it was starting to take its toll. It is a hard ride, into a beautiful but hostile environment. Any rider should seriously consider the environment and the length of the ride before going. Beginner riders should not do the longer rides, and even intermediate riders should seriously consider their physical fitness and capabilities. You do need to look after your horse, yourself and your tent, as well as helping out with other bits and pieces around camp. Personally, all this comes naturally; a campsite encourages everyone to pitch in and the camaraderie that results is one of the highlights. Another observation is to make sure you watch your water intake and sunscreen application. This is seriously the ride of a lifetime. I can't speak highly enough of Rancho Cactus.

review_text: I almost missed going to Cerro Santa Lucia while in Santiago, but I am so glad I stopped by. It is a "park" on a hill in a great, bustling neighborhood (Barrio Lastarria). There are beautiful fountains, interesting architecture, and numerous cobblestone stairways that you can explore. The top offers nice views of the city and the mountains (on a clearer day), but it's tiny and crowded up there. I recommend taking some time to people-watch on one of the lower patios instead. I hung out on the north side and the mountain views from there were also great. I was worried I needed tennis shoes from what other reviews noted, but really you're fine in any shoes that are not stiletto heels. Be sure to also check out the Centro Artesanal Santa Lucia across the street, where you can find jewelry and other Chilean trinkets. I walked up and down Cerro San Cristobal the other day and while it's a much higher hill with better views (and thus takes WAY longer), I found Cerro Santa Lucia to be a far more interesting and enjoyable "cerro" experience.

review_text: Torres del Paine is breathtaking! We did it in 4 nights. I found it hard to find a lot of concrete info on planning the hike, so here is a summary of what we did for people looking to plan the hike. Day 1: Bus from PN to the park. Bus tickets are readily available & can be bought in most hostels. All morning buses leave at either 7:30 or 7:50. They get to the park at the same time. The 7:50 bus has a shorter breakfast stop, so it catches up to the earlier buses. We traveled in low season so we had no problem booking tickets the night before, but we were told that in high season you might want to book them a few days in advance. The cost is 15,000 pesos return per person (about $30USD). Bus stops at park entrance (Laguna Armaga) and you pay about 18,000 pesos per person for admission. After this some people stay on the bus and continue to catch the catamaran and others get off and start the hike from Laguna Armaga. We chose the latter. From entrance of the park you can take a minibus (for 2,500 pesos per person) to the start of the hike. Or if its nice weather we can walk the 7km along a dirt road. We walked and it ended up being a nice warm up before we hit the trail. Once we got to the begging of the train (around the Torres Central hostel) it was all straight up for several hours. We stayed at Chileno Refugio the first night. We were not rushing on the walk that day and we arrived at Chileno at around 2:30PM Day 2: Early wake-up at 3:45AM, quick breakfast and off to hike to the base of the Torres to witness the amazing sunrise. This is totally worth it. But make sure to bring a good headlamp since part of this up-hill hike can be treacherous! Arrive for sunrise around 6AM. Back down to Refugio by 9:30. Pick up our big packs and off to Los Cuernos Refugio. This is mostly downhill, but still a long walk. We arrived at Cuernos at 3:30PM. Day 3: Wake up, quick breakfast and off to Italiano campsite to drop our big bags and walk up French Valley. Walk from Cuernos to Intaliano is about 1.5 hours, walk up and down French Valley is about 5 hours. After which we picked up our packs and headed to Lodge Paine Grande (another solid 2 hours). Day 3: leisurely morning at Paine Grande, set off to Refugio Grey at 10AM. A lot of people do this as a day trip from Paine Grande. I would recommend (if you have the time) to go up to Refugio Grey and do the extra hike to get a great view of the glacier. Arrived in Refugio Grey at 1pm. Dropped off packs and walked to the Glacier mirador - 3 hours return. Definitely worth it! Day 4: up early, out by 8am, walked back go Paine Grande and caught the catamaran at 12:30PM. There is a lot of talk about which direction to go - for us the decision was simple. We took a look at the weather forcasts and saw that for our first 2 days at the park the weather was going to be spectacular. So we decided to do the hardest (and very beautiful) part of the walk first. There is absolutely nothing wrong with doing it the opposite way (in fact many people will tell you to do it this way), but you really are leaving the most challenging parts of the hike to the very end. Personally, I'd rather get it over with first. In terms of food at the refugios - breakfasts usually consist of runny eggs, a handful of cereal (corn flakes of some sort) and some toast. Lunches are by far the worst meals - the sandwiches all the refugios give you to go are gross - mostly mushy, soggy break with egg salad, some sort of chicken or roast beef. Dinners were by far the best meals - they are either beef or chicken, with rice or potatoes and some sort of soup and boiled veggies. We carried our breakfast & lunches with us (breakfast - instant oatmeal and there was no problem getting refugios to give us hot water and wraps, tuna and some cheese for lunches). Also, bring lots of money in case you want to buy snacks on the trail, since all the refugios sell snacks, wine and beer!

review_text: We read many reviews of this tour and were booked on it by AUDLEY travel. There were some not so great ones and some OK. However we found the tour interesting and well worthwhile and would not have wanted to miss it. To be fair it's a lengthy day - we were picked up at 0830 at the hotel and we then picked up a couple of other hotels ( there were only 12 on our tour ) and then we were straight off. It's about 70 minutes drive to the port where you then take a 30 minute ferry to the island. Once there you are on part dirt roads and part Tarmac and spend a bit if time in a couple of old churches and a square, then down to the beach and stop for photos along the way etc , book lunch at the beachside rstaurant which was gat, take the boat tour out to the islands to see seal, all typ s of birds and ducks and of course nesting penguins of both Magellan and Humboldt - the only place in the Pacific you can see both together. Back to the shore to have lunch which you spare book, then on to a museum of local cultural information and then drive back getting back to Puerto Varas around 1930. So long day. But if you want to see this stuff and you only come once in my view it's worth it. We could have paid 75$ each and traveled on a private tour as a couple and paid all entrance fees and ferry separately and the boat trip to the islands. But for the price charged by these guys I thought it was worth while. If it had been a large coach with 50/60 people on it I am not sure it would have been as enjoyable but maybe we just picked the right day. Our guide Eduardo was great and was able to answer every question we threw at him.

review_text: An easy and really pleasant venture out of the city via the Metros' Red Line. It costs only between 700 and 800 pesos (around $1 us) and takes about 20 minutes from the area around Plaza de Armas. It's et up like a small village, with dirt paths meandering past approx. 200 shops made of mud and straw. Everything is nestled under trees and foliage with an ample amount of seats set up in picturesque spots. Here you can take a rest, soak up some sun and listen to the peacefulness. Everything from shrubbery and rabbits to lapis lazuli jewelry, copper wares, wood and ceramics products. All tastefully crafted. I spent a couple of hours here. Just wandering, checking the wares and in some cases watching the artists at work. There's places to eat, have cold drinks and ice-creams. An additional fascinating extra of this market is the permanent bonsai garden and insects display. There's a whole wall of preserved insects and butterfly's behind glass cases. The species come from all over the world, Africa, Australia, Asia and South America. The shear size and beautiful colors of these creatures had me completely mesmerized.

review_text: I booked A Bite of Santiago about a week before my trip, and this was to be my first introduction to Santiago. The day before the trip, Urban Adventures Santiago emailed to say I was the only one booked and they would be happy to run it for just me, but if I didn't feel comfortable on my own they would refund my money. I was more than happy to do this on my own, nothing like having your own personal tour guide. Maria was fantastic during the entire trip - extremely knowledgable, very interesting and a fantastic guide. Because I was on my own we were able to improvise a little when the queues to San Cristobal were very long - I wasn't keen on standing in the sun for an hour - so we decided on Santa Lucia Hill instead. From a food perspective, the morning stop was at the market where I had my first (and not my last) taste of Pisco Sour, and also my first Empanada. Both were very tasty and by the end of the week I had enjoyed quite a few more Pisco Sours! Lunch was at Galindo near San Cristobal Hill, with Pastel de Choclo on the menu. This was another great local dish which I thoroughly enjoyed. What I loved about this trip was the combination of history and local food - being able to taste things you would probably never try without local knowledge. I thoroughly enjoyed this trip - am very pleased I did it. Maria was outstanding.
