review_text: I visited this place with my husband on weekend. Now, we have no kids, so this was really just the two of us. However, I love these type of interactive science museums so we decided it would be fun. The majority of people were with kids, but there were definitely other adults there too. Quite a mix actually. When you first get there, you´re asked to signup for any of the "extra" activities they offer. I think 2 or 3 are included in your entrance ticket. We arrived a little late - around noon - and many of the activities were already full. We were able to signup for the simulated earthquake exhibit, and something related to space. The museum itself is quite extensive. They have several different areas, each with many different stations or exhibits. As the name implies, almost everything is interactive. It took us about 2 hours to go around the museum (not including the 2 extra activities), and we didn´t look at everything in great detail, only the ones that were more interesting to us. I think if you did, you´d be there all day! The earthquake simulation was quite interesting. First you spend about 20 minutes going around an exhibit that explains the science behind earthquakes, along with one of the tour guides. After that, you go to the simulation. I wasn´t living in Santiago in February 2010 during the earthquake, so it was definitely an experience. It´s a very strong movement, and it lasts quite a while. I don´t really remember too much about the second activity, on space, so I´m not sure what that says about it. We did go about 10 months ago, but I remember walking out not feeling too impressed with it, compared to the rest of the museum. Overall, I think this is a very well done museum that kids and adults alike will enjoy. I would highly recommend it!

review_text: Salar de Atacama is my third salt flat, after Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia and Salinas Grandes in Argentina. All three salt flats are very different and warrant a visit, if only just to get different perspectives and photo opportunities. While not as large as Uyuni, Atacama holds its own with its stunning rock-like salt terrain (Uyuni boasts flat, hexagonal salt slabs). Most tour groups stop along the main road for a couple of obligatory photo opportunities. I did the tour with Pachamama by Bus and the driver drove us all the way into the heart of the flats, using a smaller and less-traveled road only used by mining trucks for some of the best scenery in the salt flats.

review_text: This small museum rates as one of the great museums of the world for the quality of its exhibits and the care of its curation. It was the top priority on my trip to Santiago and I was not disappointed. The masterpiece collection on the top floor certainly lives up to its name. I visited on a Tuesday ( it’s closed on Mondays) and there was no difficulty accessing the upper galleries, as some earlier reviewers experienced. Throughout the upper galleries there is quite a lot of English explanation, though some people might have missed it because it comes last in the 4 panels that typically introduce the different areas being a examined in each subsection. It’s less detailed than the Spanish language information, of course, but adequate for non-specialists. Don’t miss the small, dimly lit room dedicated to weaving. It contains some priceless pieces many hundreds of years old. Cloth is more perishable than ceramics and metals, so a lot rarer, but this wonderful collection suggests how very colourful the pre-Columbian scene must have been. Finally, the cafe downstairs is great, especially if you are looking for good quality vegetarian or vegan food. If you are interested in pre-Colombian America ignore the suggested 1 hour. I spent over 90 minutes upstairs alone.

review_text: In all of my travels in South America, this is one of the most impressive display of military buildings and monuments in one location. The Armada de Chile, the Chilean Navy Building, which fills the south southwest corner of the Plaza Sotomayor, with its massive Mansard style archtecture, is the headquarters for the Chilean Navy. Across the plaza stands the Monument of the Heroes. A few blocks away, numerous ships of the Chilean Navy are docked. This facility stands in gigantic contrast to the small wooden Armada de Chile outpost at Easter Island, some 2,200 miles to the west at Hanga Roa.

For the private foody tour, Colin met us at the Mercado Central and walked us around the area. He was a great host/guide and very thoughtful about the items he selected. He seemed to be constantly tailoring the excursion to our preferences.We tried smoothies at the market, Hogs, a great cocktail bar with tapas, and a wine bar called bocanaris which was excellent. I loved that it was by foot so we could get a sense for the neighborhoods. For the Wine tour and Valparaiso/Vina del Mar excursion, we had a different guide, Alvaro, who was hand selected by Colin and did an equally fantastic job. Our driver (I apologize i'm blanking on his name) was great as well-- expert on wine and gave some additional color along the way. In the planing phases, we were able to select the vineyard we wanted to go to and make it a tailored event. We absolutely adored the Kingston vineyard and greatly enjoyed our experience there. After the wine tour and tasting, we drove out to Valpairaiso for a delicious/scenic lunch overlooking the water. Our tour guide was always happy to double as a photographer and stop for us to take pictures and admire the sights. He made stops along the way to pick up water bottles, treats, and even a local magazine (Condorito) to show us another culture staple of Chile. Learned a lot and had a ton of fun. Would definitely recommend to anyone looking to better understand Santiago/Chile. Review of: Small-Group Santiago Food and Market Tour Including Mercado Central Thank you for your review and for booking our tours! Everyone comes down here with a much different background and for much different reasons, so we pride ourselves on our ability to adjust in the private tours to these differences, as they are what makes it all so interesting. Hope the rest of your time in Chile has been good, all the best!

review_text: Recently, I was in Chile and made three trips with your company: two days in the Farellones Park and one day in Valparaíso. He was little communicative and barely stopped at the venues so we could take pictures and record the moments. In addition, Mr. Will mentioned a boat ride that would only take place if all passengers in the van agreed. Despite our requests for more information about this activity, the Guide avoided clarifying the details. We ended up paying R$ 60.00 per person to see the sea lions, but we were quite frustrated, because the experience was very short and we could not observe the animals properly. Subsequently, we were taken to another point where we saw the sea lions at no extra cost, which allowed us to appreciate these animals closely. During the tour to Farellones with the Guide Light, I was disappointed with the service provided. On three occasions, she simply left me talking alone and did not answer my questions. This lack of attention and education led me to give up buying two tours to wineries with your company. review_text: I usually don't write reviews but I think this recommendation can help a few people thinking about taking this tour in Santiago. Santiago its an incredible city, I definitely recommend it to anyone traveling to South America. I traveled with my father and sister to the city and we only had one day so we decided to take this tour since it was well rated and seemed interesting. We let know the guides that we only had a day in Santiago and they said that the tour was perfect for that. The tour is OK, you get to see some interesting parts of the city. The guides (Gonzalo and a Venezuelan girl) are very nice. BUT for someone coming from other Latin American country, spending more than 60 mins in a local market is a waste of time and money (if you are paying for it), even though the story is compelling, it is nothing different to what you are used to see. For someone coming from a developed country... I would not recommend it either, there are many other sites to see before taking this type of tour. What I am really did not like about the experience was the price. It is extremely expensive, trust me. The tour costs about USD 35-40 for a 3.5 hour ride in places that, as I said, are not worth it. I have been to many other bike tours in Europe and Latin America, some of them expensive but the experience are great, this one not so much. The tour guides do say that "If you are not Okey with anything about the tour, just tell us and we will reimburse you the tour fee" but to be honest, this is a too embarrassing thing to do when the guides are nice and there are other people around, it is just too expensive. I would definitely change my rating if the price was fair, in all the tour is an OK experience but not worth it for the money or time. I know it is very unusual to write such a bad review but I think that with this I am helping other people visiting Santiago.

review_text: Some local friends took me to Fuerte Bulnes and I'm glad they did. The history of the place is fascinating. Originally the main settled city of the area, settlers (50ish men and 2 women) only stayed for a few years before deciding the location exposed them too much to the elements and packing up for Punta Arenas. Given that Fuerte Bulnes sits perched on a cliff with water on three sides, I think it's safe to say the settlers' decision was founded. That being said, what's left of the fort makes some pretty spectacular views. The views are the main attraction, the buildings are interesting but simple and more or less all look the same and do not contain furnishings (besides the small chapel). From Fuerte Bulnes you can see an island where people were detained during the Dictatorship. To get there, you also pass by a seemingly inaccurate sign marking the middle of Chile and an island where many settlers starved without food. My trip here was substantially improved by all of these explanations that I got from friends. If you don't have friends to take you, I would recommend going with a tour that leaves from Punta Arenas.

review_text: I highly recommend the family owned and operated boutique winery of Casa Marin if your looking for a quiet place to unwind. My husband and I stayed in the Jeronimo Villa our first night and then moved to the Miramar Villa for two more nights at Casa Marin. The Jeronimo Villa is a one bedroom rustic cottage in the middle of the vineyard. I much preferred the more modern Miramar Villa at the top of the hill in the vineyard with its awesome deck with brick grill, comfortable living room facing a picture window with views of the vineyard. The beds are comfortable as well. Upon arriving our first night we were escorted to our cabin and then we drove back to the main house for dinner. Dinner was simple and served with Casa Marin's excellent Pinot Noir. The villa kitchen is stocked with wine, coffee, tea and water. The following morning we walking through the vineyard and then enjoyed a cup of coffee on the deck while waiting for breakfast to be delivered to our cabin. After breakfast we took off for the coast and drove to Algorrobo for lunch. We picked up some groceries in Casablanca on our return and enjoyed a great dinner we prepared on the outdoor grill. The following day we toured the Casa Marin winery and then visited Valparaiso that afternoon. Following breakfast on our last day we toured other wineries in the Casblanca valley suggested by Maria Luz, the owner of Casa Marin, before returning to Santiago.

review_text: We booked a tour to Tierra Del Fuego + Penguin Park, and it was unfortunately one of the most disappointing tours during our trip to Patagonia. Since the ferry to Magdalena Island was not operating, we decided to take a chance on the penguin colony in Tierra Del Fuego. Our impression was that we were going to see penguins from a short distance, but instead we drove over 2.5 hours to see penguins from 100 feet away behind a glass pane in a wooden shed. We weren’t taken to the museum that other guests describe. We also didn’t go to the restaurant. Our tour guide didn’t tell us anything about the history of the indigenous people who lived in the area. It was a quiet drive to an underwhelming penguin colony and a rush back home due to the sudden onset of heavy winds. While you cannot blame the tour company for poor weather, it’s better to cancel the tour for the day, rather than have customers pay full price for a mediocre experience. This tour is a day we’ll never get back, and it’s especially disappointing, given the exceptional ratings of Turismo Selkham. If you’re in Punta Arenas, you’re better off skipping this tour if Magdalena Island is unavailable.

review_text: A visit to the modern Parque Bicentenario is well worth it for a leisurely stroll or bike ride. It is located in the heart of the Vitacura community, bordering the south side of the Mapocho river. It is rather a large park but carries a relaxing atmosphere for both locals and tourists alike. There is a large man made lagoon, with beautiful views of the water and city skyline & on a clear day the majestic Andes can be seen in the distance. The Lagoon, is also home to numerous black necked swans as well as other unusual fowl and fish. Children and adults alike, can be seen feeding the birds at all times. A lovely park to visit if you have time.

review_text: We connected with Jose and his team through cross referencing wine tour reviews for Chile and Argentina. Uncorked focusses on the Chilean Wine experience with addition of available cooking classes. After reviewing possible tours and combinations, we booked for a cooking class, 4 days of wine tours, and some hotel/airport transfers as well. All arrangements went very smoothly with prompt attention to time and distance. Cooking Class: Our chef and market tour guide Eliana was great. Wonderful experience wandering through the fish, vegetable and meat markets of Santiago. Quite the sight of some of the freshest foods available. This was a smaller group of about 10 people and was quite easy to manage. After shopping we voted on taking the subway back the kitchen for the class. Great choice of menus selections, very interactive, everyone getting a chance to help with preparations and plating. Great wine selections starting with our new favorite drink, the Chilean Pisco Sour. Day 1 Wine tour: Colchagua Valley: Clos Apalta, Neyen de Apalta, lunch and tasting at Viu Manent, the Rayuela Wine and Grill. Jose picked us up right on time at our vineyard hotel in Santa Cruz to start our first tour of the beautiful Colchagua Valley. These were arranged as private tours for 4 people. We had discussed before our trip of seeing the smaller, family, boutique or unique wineries and Jose certainly delivered. Wonderful wine and Jose was very knowledgeable about the region, the people and the wines. Chile is not just Carménère! Day 2 Wine Tour: Colchagua Valley: Vina Escodida, Lunch and tasting at Casa Silva, Alchemy Wines. Jose once again came through with some spectacular choices. From very small family owned start up, to beautiful established boutique winery to garage wine. Seriously, barrel tasting of some the best of the region with a very young winemaker. Great choices, great people. Day 3 Wine Tour: to San Antonio Valley: Vina Chocalan, Lunch and tasting at Matetic, Casa Marin. This time the day was hosted by Andrea and she was also very knowledgeable about the region and which of the wines were presenting very well. Great day! We had also arranged for them to drop us in Vina Del Mar for the last few days of our Chilean experience. Day 4 Wine Tour: to Casablanca Valley: Bodegas Re, Attilio & Mochi, Lunch and tasting at House of Morande. Back with Jose again for a tour of a very different, and yet beautiful valley. Overall this is a dedicated, small team of knowledgeable wine and food folks. All of the recommendations for restaurants in the area, shopping, wineries and events were spot on for our tastes. We would all highly recommend using them for any of your trips to Chile. Review of: Best Wine Tasting in Santiago

review_text: This tour is usually done in conjunction with the Valle del Arco Iris. It is one of the largest collections of rock art in the area of San Pedro de Atacama and where we had our first lesson of the day on the traces of the people of Atacama dating up to 10,000 years ago (it is worth the tour with a guide). The site would be a resting point for the lowly peoples in their nomadic phase, with four distinct petroleum/pictoglyph styles left by them. Many of the images on this site feature representations of lamas or alpacas. In the older pertoglyphs, the limbs of the lamas are represented only by straight lines, as in a child's drawing (very small child). As time passes, petroglyphs and pictoglyphs evolve, showing animals with a higher level of detail.

review_text: The Colchagua Valley is the most popular wine district with the most famous Chillean wineries. I was greatly looking forward to my visit. Until I got there and saw how things are run. The entire process is designed to separate you from as much money as possible. You must register and reserve winery visits, even if you have your own car. Each visit involves a mandatory tour (and riding in a horse-drawn cart on bumpy dirt trails, under the hot sun isn't that much fun). The "tours" are quite expensive, some as high as $45 or $50 per person (leave any non-drinkers back at the hotel). The "tours" are deliberately inefficient, so you can only visit two or perhaps three wineries in a day - they suggest you spend three or four days in the Valley (two days is plenty). Maps are deliberately unavailable, roads are essentially unmarked with poor or no signs. The people at the wineries are quite nice and friendly, but you have to get away from the hucksters in Santa Cruz. I guess I was lucky, but I went on a Summer weekend, and using maps in my guidebooks, went directly to the wineries I wanted and talked my way in. Had a fantastic lunch at Viu Manent and all the wineries were practically deserted. I realize you need to respect the local culture, but I have visited wineries all over the World and this is one of the strangest, most poorly organized, and overpriced wine country trips I ever made. Not all gringos like to spend hundreds do dollars for very little ...

The actual name of the falls are the Cascada de Ventisquero Colgante. They’re found along the Carretera Austral in Chilean Patagonia. How to get there? The town is situated along the Carretera Austral. It’s the gateway to the hanging glacier falls. Take a bus to get there. That’s if you don’t have your own set of wheels. - Heading north to Puyuhuapi: As of February 2020, in peak season, Buses Terraustral run a daily 3pm service from Coyhaique to Puyuhuapi. This costs $9,000CLP ($10.50USD). It arrives around 8pm. Bus timetables quickly change, so visit their website for the latest. Please find the link above. - Heading south to Puyuhuapi: Buses Terraustral leave Chaitén at 4pm on Mondays, Wednesdays & Fridays. Price is $6,000CLP ($7USD). It arrives in Puyuhuapi around 7pm. How to get to Queulat National Park Even some very recent blogs seemed to refute the existence of a dedicated shuttle bus that goes to and from the Queulat National Park. However, as of February 2020, we can assure you that such a bus does exist. At least during peak season. We arrived in Puyuhuapi around 8pm from Coyhaique and were able to buy a ticket for the bus upon arrival. Here, we were lucky enough to get the last 2 seats available on the bus heading to the National Park the following day. The bus departs at 9am from outside their shop for $5,000CLP/person ($6USD) and returns at 3pm. So we recommend buying your shuttle bus tickets ASAP after arriving in Puyuhuapi. But if they are sold out, never fear! We saw a couple rock up in the morning wanting tickets. Becaue they were sold out, they were redirected to another shuttle bus service that had availability. The hanging glacier falls hike From town, the bus will initially stop at the entrance to pay the National Park fee of $8,000CLP/person ($9USD) for foreign nationals. You will then reboard and be dropped off at the start of the hike around 10-10:30am. This is more than enough time to complete the fairly easy although sometimes muddy 6.2km return hike. All we can say is it’s a huge reward for such minimal effort! The viewing platform for the falls is fairly small and can easily overcrowd. So if arriving by bus, we would recommend you hike there quickly for more peaceful viewing. You then have ample time to stroll back and even complete some of the other much smaller walks around the entrance. These are nothing to write home about. But you will definitely have time to kill waiting for the return bus. Getting out of Puyuhuapi Please note the main bus station is located on the main street. It's a tiny town so it's hard to miss. - Heading north from Puyuhuapi: Buses Terraustral leave Puyuhuapi on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays at 6am for $6,000CLP ($7USD). They arrive in Chaitén around 9am. - Heading south from Puyuhuapi: Buses Terraustral run a daily 6:20am service from Puyuhuapi to Coyhaique. This costs $9,000CLP ($10.50USD). It arrives around midday. But again, check the website to guarantee bus departure details. They become less frequent outside of peak season. Dan & Beck, Travel Made Me Do It

review_text: Hi, i just wanted to let everyone know the dangerous experience i had 2 days ago. I had walked the scenic route up this hill and headed back down the same way. It zig zags down the hill so can be in some secluded sections. I did this alone too as im a solo traveller. There is one point where there is a semi circle of benches, i went to sit down to make some notes and look at the view. A man came out of an off path and walked passed me looking at me, pretended to use the water fountain. I was already aware of danger so i stood up and as this he was about to walk up the section i came from, all of a sudden he ran towards me EXTREMELY FAST with a knife raised above his head (a hunting knife of some kind, not even a kitchen knife), it was so quick he got the bag from my shoulder and proceeded back up the off path he came. I stupidly had everything i needed in my bag, but i cant stress how terrifying it was. I had to run down the hill at least 5 mins before getting help from a a kind german dad and daughter (if you ever read this i cant thank you enough, i was laughing out of shock but it has been really traumatic since). If the guy wanted to kill me i would have been dead. Just to mention as well, before this happened, a family with 2 adult females and 3 to 4 kids was walking up the hill. Before i ran down, i almost ran up cos they were the closest, but all of a sudden that family were shouting a lot and with the name julio too. I cant decide whether they were in on it as a look out and shouting for the robber (julio) to run or they were looking down and witnessed it and were shouting to run away from the situation. It was only after i read about this happening that i want to add to the list of dangerous experiences that people have written here on tripadvisor. So, i hope this man never uses the knife he had and its always best to just hand over all your stuff as quickly as possible, because you can pay with a lot more if you put up a fight. In my situation, i didnt even have a chance to react in anyway i was totally immobilized from fear. Please nobody do this walk alone, it is a beautiful walk, but the danger involved can ruin a lot.

review_text: This is really not a good tour, I would advise people to avoid this Vineyard! We paid £30 (Sterling) Each! Firstly the tour was badly organized our hostel was not on route so we had to walk to the touristic office for pick up. For £30 English pounds I expected more than a quick spin around three bunches of vineyards a quick stop to a cellar and viewing a man forking grapes into a silver pallet! There was also too many people on our tour about 18 people in total. The tour guide was not interested in people taking in the ambiance of the vineyard as people walking slowly or taking picture were left behind the group thus missing out. Thirdly the wine tasting was pathetic! All 18 or so of us had to stand quite cosily around one table where our “expert” wine guru explained to us if the wine was “full” or “sharp”!Guru??The wine portions were again pathetic. Having experienced many French vineyards all of varying standard, this vineyard has not even come close to the lowest standard of French vineyard I have experienced all at a fraction of the price offered here. If you have the slightest interest in wine please avoid this tour as it is an insult to both your wallet and pallet!

review_text: Although I had already done a wine tour while in Santiago, Chile, I decided to do another one on a free Sunday morning. I'm glad I did because this wine tour to Santa Rita was among the best I've ever experienced. The estate is very old and the buildings comfortable to walk through. The grounds are extensive but not quite as beautiful as some other wineries in Chile but what made this tour very interesting was its detailed nature. The guide was very well trained; gave a great deal of history of the area and knew a lot about wine making. We were taken to four different aging cellars including the oldest built in the very early days of this winery featuring a natural stone cave like structure. We also saw the huge fermentation tanks and finally the wine bottling plant. During the tasting session, we were given tips how to smell and taste the wine in great detail. Although I have been on tours in other countries and am an old hand at drinking wine, I did learn some new things. The tastings included some of their moderate wines and although I can buy some Santa Rita wines here, these were some excellent choices. All told, a very good experience. And, by the way, if you are going to do only one wine tour while in Santiago, go here and not to Concho y Toro which is the more famous one that most hotels recommend.

review_text: Lake Llanqihue is the second largest lake in Chile (860 km2) situated in the southern Los Lagos Region. Its main affluents are Blanco, Pescado and Tepú rivers and the only effluent is the Maullín river. The lake has a fan-like form because of successive piedmont glaciers. The lake´s spectacular views of the the Osorno and Calbuco volcanoes make the surrounding cities/towns Puerto Varas, Frutillar, Puerto Octay and Llanquihue great tourist "must see" spots. Also a must are Ensenada and Las Cascadas spas. This lake was discovered by the first Governor of Chile, Pedro de Valdivia in 1552. You may rent a car or hire a tour. There are few bathroom facilities, therefore you need to go to a restaurant (but you have to eat there)

review_text: My husband and I, who are both nearing 50 years of age, had an amazing time completing the Circuito last week. The trip was perfectly organised by Dittmar Adventures, who also provided a guide and a porter to carry our camping and personal stuff. Our hike started from the CONAF Administrative Center, and the circuit completed at The Refugio Paine Grande, where we took the catamaran and bus back to Puerto Natales. Our trek took 9 days, and we slept in refugios (5 nights) and campsites (3 nights). We experienced all the 4 weather seasons during our trek there, so to be prepared is essential - including gloves! The W part of the trek was busy, but once we got off into the back part of the park, we knew we were in for a treat. The park was astoundingly beautiful - glaciers, the different flora and fauna, the geological varieties, the different lakes and rivers - provided us with different sceneries each day. Our guide, who used to work as a ranger in the park, was so knowledgeable and was very keen to share his passion. He was attentive, professional and very easy going, and that made the whole trekking experience more enjoyable. His interaction with the local staff also provided us some 'privileges', such as having to stay in a room all to ourselves. One point worth mentioning is our stay at the Refugio Dickson. It's location was so perfect, and the accommodation very clean, with lovely hot showers. And the surprise is the meals cooked by Carlos, a delicious 4 course dinner and for breakfast, we were treated to some homemade bread! Wonderful! We would recommend doing the Circuit without a doubt, more so during a less high peak season. And having a fantastic guide would make the whole experience more enriching.

review_text: We booked Hector for a private tour of Vino del Mar & Valparaiso and were very pleased. Originally there were to be four of us, but the other couple had to cancel last minute. Rather than increasing his price because there was now only two of us, Hector was kind of enough to keep the original pricing. review_text: Three of us (my 25 year old daughter, myself and a friend) were invited to visit the Kingston Family vineyards while on a two week trip to Santiago. We were picked up at our hotel in Santiago and driven to the vineyards (in the Casablanca valley) by a driver (Rodrigo del Valle) that was recommended by Courtney Kingston. When we arrived Courtney spent over an hour walking us around through the arbors and winemaking plant. All of us then spent another hour in the vineyards "tasting room" sampling the wine selections offered by the vineyard, and also discussing the goals of the vineyard and Courtney's wine philosophy. Total cost = zero (except lunch later and the driver). We all had a super time--very informative, very relaxed and I cannot recommend this visit highly enough--it was the best visit to a vineyard I've ever had, and I've done many throughout the world..

review_text: I would not recommend this tour agency, but after reading many other reviews all the tour agencies might just be terrible. Also be aware this agency charges much more online, if you must book with them do it in person. I’ll start with the positive, the driver drove safely and was not drunk. The accommodation and food were acceptable. The negatives, the car must have been at least 15 years old, the air conditioning pumped out hot air, when you are taking tourists in a tour of the desert you need to have working A/C. The back seat was super cramped with no leg room at all. They messed up the sun raise over the salt flats by rushing us to the top of cactus island, it’s much worse for taking pictures then watching it on the salt flats. They did not provide shoe covers when we went to the salt flats for the water, the driver then told us that when they advertise the water they provide them but not now, that’s a total lie, this was the beginning of February, the middle of rainy season and the biggest draw of the tour is the water over the salt flats causing the mirror effect. We asked about storing our bags at their uyuni office after our tour ended and they said no problem. Well they close the office at 4pm so you can only store then for an hour or two after the tour ends. The office in San Pedro closes at 8/9pm so I figured this one would close at the same time. They know most people are taking an overnight bus so joy providing luggage storage is not very helpful. Also for some reason all the tours pick you up before 7am and have you get to the Chilean boarder before 8 am, then you sit in the car and wait till around 10 am in our case to cross the boarder, why not just arrive later? They also charged us 32,000 peso more for the private room the first night, but we found out the actual cost was 200 Bolivian(around 22,000 peso). The hotel the second night was alright but I don’t understand what everyone raves about, it’s still very basic, they don’t even provide WiFi even tho the other hotels in the area do and there is cell phone signal. Also don’t provide constant hot water the second night or constant power, they only have the power in from 6-11pm and then again for like 30 minutes before you leave in the morning.

review_text: We were lucky that our tour arrived in time for breakfast in the hut, rather than in the carpark - it was minus 12 and the thought of eating outside didn't hold much appeal. Only about 7 groups can eat in the hut, so you're just lucky if you're one of them. The geyser field is set against a stunning setting of the snowy volcanoes behind them. Paths are well marked & it's very safe now (after a couple of incidents years ago). As soon as the sun came up, it transformed both the atmosphere & the temperature. We only saw one geyser erupting, and it was pretty tame. Didn't go for a swim, but enjoyed watching the other adventurous ones. The ride down was great (going up was pitch black & you couldn't see anything). Saw flamingoes, active volcanoes, llamas, stopped at a beautiful viewpoint overlooking a half frozen lagoon with big white birds in it. We were well prepared for the freezing temperatures but it didn't prevent my toes from feeling frozen, and my fingers suffering when I had to take my glove off to take a photo. Loved the trip & would thoroughly recommend it.

review_text: Actually the statue of the virgin Mary is just a small part of the park. It is nice as a viewpoint over the city and perhaps to observe religious worship. For me the highlight of the Cerro San Cristobal was to hike through what is left of nature in the vast city landscape of Santiago. Starting at the Southern foot of the hill you can hike up either Northwest or along the Eastside, most of the time through beautiful forest. I took the Eastern route and went up West towards the ridge which can be followed until the statue. Then down along the well kept trail on the West side of the hill. It took me just over 2 hours. Take water with you and some protection against the sun.

review_text: Antares has tried to get a chokehold on Torres Del Paine guides trips, but at best they’re not necessary. And at worst, their guided trips are an exercise in frustration. First off, they’re expensive and you could do the same trip yourself for far far cheaper. The profits don’t go to anyone local, they’re an expensive operation that just cashes in on the local resources but returns almost nothing back. The hotels they use are not actually even in the park...they’re located outside the entrance so a 45 min drive (in good weather, longer in bad) from the hiking trails. And worse still, on the last hiking day, they’re too cheap for even these, so put their clients up in a barebones place in Puerto Natales. The guide was a total novice. And though a nice guy and easy going, was utterly useless as a guide. Worse than being a hapless leader, he actually got in the way. His simple mistakes actually cost us time in the park. He screwed up the catamaran in the morning so we were forced to start our hike only two hours later. When you’ve only got two actual days in the park (their talk makes it sound like more but in reality this is all the time that they give in the park) two hours is a big deal. The guide has no emergency training, doesn’t even have basic first aid supplies. In other logistic situations, we had to arrange things and the guide only gave excuses why we couldn’t do things rather than solving the issue and making things happen. Antares is a useless operation that specializes in charging a lot gut cheating out on any actual services it’s supposed to provide.

review_text: So, I have lived in Barrio Bella Vista for almost two years and in the city for over six, and I still found interesting places and moments to capture on my digitized "film." This is not your regular tour where as group you follow the tour guide with a yellow umbrella and listen to her talk and then move along to the next point. The tour started with short coffee talk on a basic review of photography rules and examples of when it works to break them. Then we were given thematic clues meant to stimulate ideas and let loose in the city. We had the choice to go alone or with others from the group, to shoot a lot or just a few of the clues as we leisurely strolled where we choose to following the map or not. And then what was really personally rewarding was that we got to meet back up and show off our hall of fame (or shame) shots with an informal critique with wine ;) Overall, a delight! Thank you FotaRuta. I see my neighborhood differently now.

review_text: We did this trek (4 days, 3 nights and ~71.5 kms of hiking) in January 2016 with Chile Nativo as we were a little time poor, as long as you can pre arrange your bed in the Refugio's or are wanting to camp you can easily complete this trek in guided. We were there in January and experienced snow and some extreme wind along with a couple of beautifully sunny days so pack to cover extremely changeable conditions. Even if you are not sleeping in the Refugio's you can buy drinks etc. from them or buy your meals so if you are camping that may help out what you need to carry. Travelling in the direction from the Towers to the Grey Glacier you can leave your gear at higher camps on day 1 and day 3 as the trails are out and back removing the need to carry your packs up to the top viewing point of the Towers and the French valley. Re the trails - we climbed and walked over some pretty uneven terrain so good foot ware is advisable. We will most definitely remember the Patagonian weather (four extreme seasons in one day), the beech forests, the uneven surfaces and the most beautiful views. Our trek ended in Puerto Natales. So much beauty and wow factor, whilst you are in the region you are below a 350km long ice shelf - this shelf is the third largest area of ice in the world and therefore also fresh water resource. It feeds hundreds if not thousands of Glaciers.

review_text: We had a free morning in San Pedro, and so decided to book an astronomy tour for the night before. The Moon was almost full, so we knew we wouldn’t get the full astronomical experience, but still we hoped to enjoy a pleasant “Astrolunar” tour with knowledgeable guides and perhaps some tasty snacks. After doing some research, and finding that several of the main tours weren’t running (because of the Moon), we settled on Mitampi due to the several excellent reviews here on Tripadvisor, many of which mentioned a great guide called Diego. Unfortunately our experience didn’t live up to those reviews. Mitampi didn’t run the tour themselves, but sent us (without explaining this clearly) to join a tour run by a different agency,”Atacama Rock and Tours”. The tour was not very good. First of all, there were over 30 people on it, and only two small (12”) telescopes, meaning observation time per person was very limited. In addition, the astronomy guides on this tour were very poor, making dozens of (unintentionally) hilariously wrong statements about the celestial bodies in view. Finally, the snacks on offer were also poor, mostly industrialised biscuits and cakes, and even chicken nuggets (!). They did offer pisco and wine, and there was some nice music, but that’s about it. Moral: if booking an astronomy tour with Mitampi, make sure to ask who is actually running it.

review_text: Not worth your time or money!!! Our group of 11 booked this excursion as a convenient way to explore a winery close to Santiago and try delicious Chilean wines. We were disappointed with how logistically inefficient the transport was and felt that the winery experience was very commercial with too little time to explore and enjoy. We did not know that there were two pick-up stops. After we were picked up from the first stop at 8am, we left at 8:20am and drove 20 minutes in the opposite direction of the winery (only 50 minutes from stop one) to pick up at stop two in Vitacura. We arrived at the winery at 10am and were told to be back on the bus at 12:30pm. At the winery, we were met with a tour guide who showed us around the estate and cellars. This was cool but took 1.5 hours, followed by a 40 minute wine tasting. This only left 20 minutes to enjoy and explore on our own!! We were hoping to relax as a group, enjoy a bottle of wine, explore the museum included with our ticket, etc but couldn’t do any of that due to how commercial and structured this experience was. On top of that, they didn’t even drop us off back at stop 1!! They told us to take the bus - we ended up ubering in groups. Not cool to not disclose this in advance. $75 USD is an absolute rip-off for this sham of an experience. FWIW, I saw a brochure in my hotel (Novapark) list a similar experience for only $45 USD. We chose their Panoramic Andes tour for the first day and worked together to create a customized tour for the second which ended with being dropped off at our cruise ship in Valparaiso. Perfect! For the Panoramic Andes trip we had Fran, co-owner of ILoveChile, as our guide and Gonzolo as the driver of our comfortable mini bus. Our drive from downtown Santiago through the Maipo Canyon to the high Andes was the perfect balance of discussion, sightseeing, music and stops. Fran was a wealth of information first providing some insight into Chile's social unrest and culture as we drove through the city, and then turning to Andes geology, flora and fauna, local customs and tradition as well as industry as we drove through the country side. We passed through small towns and charming homes in the Maipo Canyon and made a picturesque stop along the river for refreshments before heading to the high Andes. We saw incredible scenery as Fran pointed out the features and named the mountain peaks and volcanoes for us. Our furthest stop was at about 6,000 feet where we took a short hike up for better views of peaks rising to over 18,000 feet. The sense of grandure in these mountains was awesome. Although we were not able to include the El Yeso Reservoir in our itinerary as the road was closed due to a recent landslide, our alternate stop for the wine tasting was in a picturesque valley surrounded by towering mountains with a view of grazing horses. While we stretched our legs and took photos, Fran set the table for our local wine tasting and snacks. We were able to spot Condor and Caracara here. Following our "cocktail" hour, we headed to a local resaurant for a typical Chilean lunch. Fran explained the entrees which were offered that day. We had the opportunity to taste dishes we might not have known to choose. Lunch consisted of bread, salad, our entree and dessert, all homemade, typical Chilean and delicious. Throughout the day Fran dug into her bag of suprises offering us bottles of water, candies, snack bags of chips and gifts. We had a game competition with prizes as well as quiet time listening to local music. It was a long day and drive but well worth it. Our second day began a bit later in the morning and took us in the opposite direction to Isla Negra, the seaside home of Pablo Neruda, and to a wine tasting at Indomita Vineyards. We had both ILoveChile owners this day with Seba driving and both Fran and Seba offering commentary. It was an equally enjoyable day through totally different scenery - vineyard valleys, euculyptus forrests, coastal mountains and the Pacific Ocean. At La Casa de Isla Negra, we had a self guided tour with personal audio sets through the home and collections of Chile's most famous and beloved literary figure. It was incredibly interesting and informative. We were able to walk through the parklike grounds surrounding the structures and enjoy the spectacular ocean views. Lunch was again included and we stopped at a cute restaurant in a forest, a place where the local families would go to eat. Indeed there were many families dining. It was another three course meal and we had the opportunity to enjoy a different entree and dessert. Following lunch we were taken to the beautiful Indomita Winery where we tasted 3 wines of our choice, enjoyed the views from their hilltop perch and were able to purchase bottles if we wished. As others have commented before us, Fran & Seba began as guides for two days but ended up as friends. They provided everything we needed, answered all our questions and dropped us off that evening at the Valparaiso Passenger Terminal with warm wishes and hugs. I highly recommend ILoveChile tours for any excursions within Santiago and Valparaiso or through the surrounding areas. You won't be disappointed. Review of: Valparaiso Day Trip from Santiago - Private Tour for Small Groups

review_text: Great company to do the trip with. 90,000 pesos + 10,000 to take a short chairlift (you can skip this and walk but I wouldn’t recommend - it’s a long day) Super professional and friendly office. Good equipment and description of the day. We had 16 in the group (I think) with plenty of guides included. This proved to be a good thing as we had a number of drop outs during the trip who were taken back professionally. Hike itself is NOT to be underestimated. I’m an active hiker (having recently done a number of 8 hour hikes through New Zealand) and this was definitely as hard if not harder than all of them (think tongariro crossing). The route is not that difficult itself but once that wind picks up there is a very real chance of a gust throwing you down that slope (does not happen regularly but you can certainly feel that slight fear as you go). Stopped maybe 4 times on the way up for a rest and pictures. Great views. The descent is via a number of bobsleigh like slides - very unique. This is the one thing that makes all that hard work very rewarding! All in all highly recommended, just be prepared to push through a bit of tiredness and fear if the wind is above 50km/h

review_text: This was my favourite place near San Pedro. Being able to float in the water was a unique experience for me. We took an afternoon tour and it was pretty busy (laguna Cejar was closed) but we stayed towards closing time so were able to get a few photos with noone in the background. Some tips that would have been helpful if going with a tour company 1. The first and last lagoon you can swim in. I recommend taking a few photos at the first lagoon and then walk towards the last lagoon as it's alot bigger. 2. We had 1.5hr here and they recommend you only swim for 20mins max, we thought what are we going to do for the other 1hr. From the first lagoon to the last one is not very close at all. And some of the path is on rocks so WEAR SHOES. I made the mistake of changing to sandals when the tour company drop us off and i got a few cuts 3. I was in for max 5 mins before my skin started hurting. Not sure if this was a combination of going in the hot springs at El Tatio that was too much for my skin 4. The walk back is pretty far, and need to account that the bus drops you off close to the first lagoon but you need to walk back to the shower/ ticket area as the tour picks you up from here 5. Showers close at 5pm sharp and trust me you will want to have a shower to wash at least some of the salt off your skin 6. Make sure you bring warm clothes as after the tour we stop for some drinks and snacks and it gets pretty windy and cold

And some of the path is on rocks so WEAR SHOES. I made the mistake of changing to sandals when the tour company drop us off and i got a few cuts 3. I was in for max 5 mins before my skin started hurting. Not sure if this was a combination of going in the hot springs at El Tatio that was too much for my skin 4. The walk back is pretty far, and need to account that the bus drops you off close to the first lagoon but you need to walk back to the shower/ ticket area as the tour picks you up from here 5. Showers close at 5pm sharp and trust me you will want to have a shower to wash at least some of the salt off your skin 6. Make sure you bring warm clothes as after the tour we stop for some drinks and snacks and it gets pretty windy and cold

review_text: With a group of friend we came over to this winery in order to enjoy a nice picnic day, something you can do as well in several other wineries thus providing us with a good comparison. By comparison, this wineries has by far the best grounds we have seen for a picnic day. The landscaping is definitively professional and the possibilities for privacy numerous. The picnic for 2 people is sold for CLP 20,000 or USD 32. Clients of Banco de Chile get a 25% discount. The basket includes soft cheese, hard cheese, dried nuts and a bottle of their standard sparkling wine or a bottle of their Aliwen wine label. If you want a different wine, there is always the option of buying wine by the glass or a different bottle at the store. If compared to other picnic kits sold by wineries in Casablanca or Maipo, there is definitively room for improvement (likely associated to a higher price though). For instance, it would be nice if they would consider adding water, cured meats and sandwiches. All in all, a beautiful experience just 50 min from Santiago.

review_text: A long day trip out of smoky Santiago to get to Cajon del Maipo and Embalse de Yeso, a lovely blue reservoir which is fed by two other reservoirs up higher in the Andes. Our driver, Sebastian, was terrific and our guide, Tomas, while very friendly, didn't tell us much about the geology, flora and fauna, etc. as the Viator write up advertised. He spent a lot of time conversing with the people in the front of the van in a conversational tone. The rest of us couldn't hear much of anything they were talking about. This, btw, was a tour done by Ecotour. We did walk a bit at the "lake" being mindful of the trucks, tourist vans and buses driving by -- it was Sunday after all and everyone was out and about. There were a few waterfalls to drive by; our "cocktail event" was held next to the abandoned dam builders' quenset huts which are now used a public toilets - gross! We did stop in San Jose del Maipo not to learn about its culture and wander the streets as advertised, but to eat an empanada as a late lunch. Then it was back to the City. Overall the trip was, as one reviewer has already stated, underwhelming especially if you've ever been in any other mountain range or reservoir in the world. If this is your first trip to a reservoir and/or mountains you'll be thrilled.

There was an option to rent a snow vehicle as a ferry between the base camp and the springs, but that broke down the day before so we didn't get that option. As someone from sea-level with almost no hiking experience/aptitude, the hike was very slow but it was not super challenging. It took approx. 2-3 hours to hike to the springs, and the snowy Andes landscape was quiet and beautiful so it was an overall enjoyable hike. So if you're looking for a more relaxing experience, you have to earn it at the end of a beautiful hike!

review_text: we drove from el calafate. we filled the car with fuel in Esperanza on route 40 . there is another gas station about 20 minutes west of this gas station. do not rent a private car because the roads in the park are dirt roads. rent something like Honda Rav 4 or Nissan X-Trail. it takes about 5-6 hours to arrive to the hotel Hosteria Lago Tyndall including crossing the boarder. the restaurant in the boarder changes money in low rates but it is the only one which does it. the road from the crossing will take left after a few kilometers to reach the park from the south. it is a beautiful road. at the end we left from the north. not so nice but you see the waterfalls close to the northern gate. we did the Torres trek in 10 hours. must do the next day we took the boat to Grey Glacier. very very nice. the rest of the day we stopped at the falls along the main road in the park and many other view points. you need more fuel for that, and Hosteria Lago Tyndall will provide it for you. this is the only hotel that will provide you fuel because they contact an old man who brings you the fuel all over the park by request.

review_text: We had a great trip from Puerto Montt to Puerto Natales. The boat was delayed 18 hours due to high winds on the previous voyage. We knew it was a cargo ship going into this and we're pleasantly surprised with the service. Rooms are basic but adequate and the three square meals a day a more than enough. There is also a store that sells snacks etc. You meet interesting people, see stunning scenery and get your transportation south! Few things to note: - the port in Puerto Montt is not the embarkation port. There are buses that take you approx 13 kms to where the boat is. Drop your bags and then wait to board the bus - if you book online, double check your reservation - we had a AAA with bathroom so we didn't have to share toilets and showers down the hall. It consisted of two single beds, each with a reading lamp, some draws and our banjo - there's not much to do so pack a book, deck of cards and some vino : ) - enjoy the ride and go with the flow!

review_text: The night I went there was a very small group. I believe their maximum is ten but we only had five. The astrnomers who run this are extremely knowledgeable and enthusiastic about what they are doing. The ride up to the observatory from town was a little hairy because it had rained hard that day, but I've been on worse, and the driver did a great job, Once we arrived there was a short wait while they prepared everything and then ....we saw so much! Nebulae and galaxies and planets! This observatory is unusual in that, although its telescope is not as powerful as those at some nearby research facilities, you are able to actually look through it without the mediation of a computer. As we were told, most astronomy now doesn't really involved viewing through a telescope, but is physics, chemistry and mathematical modeling, so this experience is really unique. I will never forget it. Remember to check dates of availability before you go. The air is so clear and the moon so bright that there is a period before and after the full moon each month when they can't operate. I emailed them directly to confirm, as I had a very small window of opportunity, and it turned out the dates on their website were not correct so be sure to check with them!

review_text: spent a week seeing this wonderful trekking environment; one of the best I have ever experienced around the globe. It takes a long time to get there - at least 3 stops on the flight from Santiago to Punta Arenas. the walking is however quite easy compared to, say, the Himalayas, and the scenery is spectacular and unique. Accommodation is available in Refugios (like youth hostels), although we camped for at least half of the time. The wind is powerful and relentless; if you look at the map of the world you will see that it runs around the whole world before slamming into the western side of Chile. At times you can "see" the wind as it rolls down hill in very narrow but extremely fast channels of downward draught - quite scary at night in a tent as it sounds like a runaway train which will flatten your tent if you are in its path.

review_text: Other reviewers have done a wonderful job of describing the Santiago home of Nobel Prize Winner, Pablo Neruda. I wish this was the #1 on the list of attractions, because it is such an enriching experience. Even if you know nothing about Chile's history or Neruda, a visit to the house will be enjoyed. The tour guides are friendly, interactive and engaging. The gift shop is FANTASTIC! Remember, this is a gift shop, not a flea market, so shop accordingly. The small cafe serves refreshing beverages and the bathrooms are very clean. Here's one of my favorite Neruda poem's: Ode to My Socks Mara Mori brought me a pair of socks which she knitted herself with her sheepherder's hands, two socks as soft as rabbits. I slipped my feet into them as if they were two cases knitted with threads of twilight and goatskin, Violent socks, my feet were two fish made of wool, two long sharks sea blue, shot through by one golden thread, two immense blackbirds, two cannons, my feet were honored in this way by these heavenly socks. They were so handsome for the first time my feet seemed to me unacceptable like two decrepit firemen, firemen unworthy of that woven fire, of those glowing socks. Nevertheless, I resisted the sharp temptation to save them somewhere as schoolboys keep fireflies, as learned men collect sacred texts, I resisted the mad impulse to put them in a golden cage and each day give them birdseed and pieces of pink melon. Like explorers in the jungle who hand over the very rare green deer to the spit and eat it with remorse, I stretched out my feet and pulled on the magnificent socks and then my shoes. The moral of my ode is this: beauty is twice beauty and what is good is doubly good when it is a matter of two socks made of wool in winter.

review_text: We booked Portillo after stumbling upon an Instagram account run by one of the ski instructors. We were expecting views, but it took our breath away. From arrival to check out we loved our trip, despite the lack of snow, we had the most wonderful 5 days. We booked a 4-day mini week and extended for a day. We were expecting to have to change rooms but when we arrived a wonderful lady on reception offered us a free drink and said she would have everything ironed out for us in an hour. In fact we hadn't even finished our drinks before she returned to say everything was sorted. We booked a lake-view balcony and it was worth every penny! The views on the clear night we checked in were breath taking, but we were blown away the next morning at sunrise were even more beautiful. The lake has so many faces and it will show you them all over a course of a few days and different weather. We read a lot of reviews before coming and they all talked about how Portillo is like a cruise ship in the mountains. It is exactly like that and gives you those options for lodging too: basic dorms, shared cabins or hotel rooms. All options have access to the famous pools and can use the hotel facilities so something for every taste and budget. We booked the most expensive option with a balcony, 6th floor room and for us it was worth it. We had been skiing for a week before and I needed a day off, on a ski holiday I can feel guilty taking a day off but having that while catching some rays on our balcony was the a beautifully indulgent day and I have no regrets about! Unfortunately Chile experienced a snow drought this year so the pistes were not wonderful while we were there, in fact the closed the resort early just after we left, but if you love skiing there was always fun to be had. My boyfriend was captured by the lure of the Super-C before we came and I was amazed by how it captured the imagination of everyone else there too. Apres in the hot tubs is under the shadow of the Super-C climb and every evening was spent overhearing the murmurings and stories of dreamers and adventurers wondering if they could/should do it and if the snow on the other side would be worth it. We made it up and enjoyed the chalky treats on the otherside, but advice to others out there: just because its surrounded by lore do not be tempted up unless you are ready, the climb is challenging even before you come to the exposed parts. If you decide to go seek advice from others and check in with ski patrol. The hotel has a wonderful old-timey charm and retains its family run feeling. review_text: It seems to be a paradox but the Lake Llanquihue seems to begin in Puerto Varas. Going by its right edge, you can enjoy the scenic beauty of this lake, passing by Volcano Calbuco at right. In approximately 50km you will reach Ensenada where you should stop to enjoy the view. Continuing on this road, you will have access to the Park Vicente Pérez Rosales (Tramo Ensenada - Buenas Yerbas), which gives you access to the Osorno Volcano. Following this road, you will have a beautiful view of the volcano and rare formations of Columnar Basalt. Following, you will go through a series of farms that make you think being in Switzerland. After that, you will pass by small towns: Puerto Octay, Frutillar and Llanquihe. To return to Puerto Varas is necessary to access the Ruta 5 (toll) because part of this lakeside road is not completed yet (2013). Go to Lake Llanquihue and get addicted to it. I bet you'll think about moving to this place. So take the opportunity and stays in Ensenada for at least two or three days.

review_text: My wife and I spent a total of about 12 days with Caminandes. We stayed in their glamping accommodation (they also have rooms) in a park-like tranquil setting just off the main drag but accessible to everything within a 3 minute walk. Staff is very friendly and helpful. Co-owner and manager Paula is very responsive, flexible and helpful in setting up tours. We did a wide variety of tours (lakes, valleys, trekking) and all were great. All guides (Freddy, Roberto, Leon and Diego) were knowledgeable and genuinely kind people whose company we enjoyed immensely. What separates Caminandes from other agencies is that they run smaller group tours (we had between 2-6 people) and the personalized attention you receive. The food is wonderful and the service sublime. Some complicated logistics/transfers were handled flawlessly and with a smile. We could not have been more impressed. Simply put, it’s the best in town. Although they don’t offer tours to Uyuni themselves, Caminandes works with a Bolivian agency that ran a safe, fun and great trip. Caminandes has recently opened a branch in Santiago, which we used to do tours of Santiago, Valparaiso and the Maipo valley. Staff, drivers and guides there (Roi, Camilo, Pablo, Felipe and Alejandra) were of the same high quality as in San Pedro. Traveling with Caminandes felt like traveling with friends. What good fortune to have found them. We hope to return soon.

review_text: My wife and I were in Puerto Varas in the last week of May/25 and as we couldn't miss it, we went to the Osorno Volcano Ski Center. To get there there are tour packages or you can go by car. For us, the option of going by car was great, as it gave us flexibility in our schedules. Suggestion… go early. The station opened at 11:00 am and we arrived shortly after that. The parking lot is a bit messy and was already full. If you arrive later you will end up on the road and walk a long way to get up. The ski resort is simple. There are 2 (two) cable cars. One leads halfway up the mountain and the other near the top. If you're not skiing, you can go halfway. There is only snow up there… there are no bathrooms or restaurants or activities. Have fun alone playing in the snow. At the base of the station there is a small restaurant, which doesn't have many options or much space. So, take something to eat if you are going to be there for a long time. But, the view of the lake and the volcano is worth it. I recommend and would return:

review_text: We LOVED this tour! We arrived in San Pedro de Atacama a few nights before the full moon, so were really happy that we were able to do a SAT-II session with Jorge on our first night, as it was the highlight of our trip! It was absolutely incredible to see so many stars and planets with the naked eye, and then to look through one of Jorge's many telescopes and see even more stars, some thousands of light years away, was truly incredible. We saw the Milky Way stretching overhead! We saw the red eye of Jupiter and the rings of Saturn! We saw star clusters thousands of light years away! We could watch the stars move across the night sky as the planet turned, making us feel very small. It was really a fantastic evening! Jorge also really cares about making sure his guests have a great experience. We saw many companies taking people out at 9pm during the full moon. I'm not sure what they were able see with a bright moon, besides the moon itself and a couple of bright stars. But Jorge took us out at 2am, after the moon had already set, so we would have the darkest sky to see the most distant stars. This is an expensive tour for sure. If you don't care too much and just want to see a couple stars, you may be better off going with a random cheap tour in town. But if you really want to make the most of your time in one of the best stargazing locations in the world, go with Jorge. It's worth it. It is very cold, so wear all your layers (e.g. long underwear, hat, gloves, etc.). Jorge has some heaters and blankets, and his wife serves warm beverages, but it is still freezing.

review_text: After I heard the plan to wake up at 5 a.m, meet at 6 a.m, drive an hour and a half to two hours, eat breakfast there, and be in 10 degrees F, I told my husband I didn't want to go. It sounded like a terrible plan. All I can say is it would have been a shame to have missed such an experience. There is nothing like it in North America. I thought it might be like Old Faithful or the Yellowstone geysers. Not so! This whole geothermal area is quite an amazing place. You walk through the bubbling geysers, take incredible pictures, eat a picnic breakfast outside, and have one of the best experiences of your lifetime. There is a hot spring (really HOT) where you can swim. It was too cold outside for us, but there was one man swimming. What great pictures we have of a very special day. Don't miss it! I would rate it the number one attraction of the area. We stopped at a small town along the way, population FIVE, and they sell llama brochettes and hot coffee. You can see their church and a few houses and get more special pictures. If you are visiting Atacama it is definitely one of the things you have to do. GO!

review_text: If you're interested in climbing Pućon's active volcano, Villarrica, there are a ton of companies to take you to the top. I chose Sol Y Nieve because of glowing reviews on blogs, because they speak English, and because they are a friendly bunch of professionals. When you walk into their office in central Pucon, you're greeted by John, one of the friendliest and reassuring people I've met in Chile so far. On the mountain, the team were equally as friendly. For a group of 18, there were 4 or maybe even 5 guides. I felt safe with this team of pros who do this intense 4 hour trek 3-4 days a week. Feeling safe is incredibly important if you want to enjoy yourself on the volcano. It's steep at times and you want to be confident in the abilities of the guides as well as the gear the tour company provides. I was confident with both. Many many thanks for your review of your experience with Sol y Nieve. For decades now we have prided oursleves in offering a superior product than our competitors in Pucón so it is great for us to hear that that is appreciated. We do hope that one day you may return to Pucón to further explore our area.

review_text: We self-drove around the Atacama area with a truck (not 4WD) in early April after acclimatizing in San Pedro for 2 days. We left San Pedro around 10 am and arrived at El Tatio around noon. We were the ONLY people in the park, it was warm, and we still got to see all of the fumaroles and geysers. Of course the steam is more pronounced in the early morning hours and I'm sure the light is beautiful at sunrise, but we didn't feel like we missed out on anything. In fact, anything but! Our pictures are unspoiled by people, we got to see everything that the 4 am folks did, and the wildlife came out to the geyser field to visit us. Flamingos, hawks, condors, lots of other birds, lizards, vicunas... The geysers were playing like crazy while we were there. The altitude made us feel drunk and woozy (don't stand up too fast!) but otherwise we were fine to walk around (slowly). We felt 100% fine sitting down driving in the truck but odd as soon as we stood up and while sitting down to have lunch outside. The drive there and back was simply stunning. Factor in extra time for photography stops. Absolutely zero problems self-driving with Google maps offline, though it is easy to leave the park accidentally--the main road seems to just pass through the park without any signage. Stick close to the geyser field so you don't have to turn around on the twisty roads! That said, if you pass through the park and drive 5-10 min on the main road out, there is a gorgeous view of the mountains and valleys beyond the park. There is a turnaround spot, though it's still a bit tight, and you'll definitely have to be careful and do a 4-6 point turn! It seems as though they smooth the road out after all the tours have passed through--we saw two tractors at work, going opposite directions. It was nice to drive on the smooth road that they had worked on. There is one spot early on in the drive where you need to ford a small, rocky stream. We saw a few cars out so it seems like it is a doable drive with a car, however we felt safer driving to the Atacama sights with our truck. The road is still very rough, with tons of washboard (the sections where the tractors hadn't gotten to yet).

review_text: The salar de Tara is about 3.5 hours from San Pedro, towards the border with Argentina. After a bumpy ride in the desert you will end up in a crazy, barren landscape where here and there are scattered rock formations carved in ancient volcanic debris. And then you reach a place where you look downhill and see the laguna, with different colors based on depth and salt concentration, and the volcano chain in the background. There are often geese and duck nesting on the shore. A short walk downhill will take you to a picnic area (all the tours gather here) where most people feel like they're having lunch on another planet. It's very likely that you will see viscachas (big rabbits) hiding in the obsidian debris all around.

review_text: We visited the Marble Caves in Feb, 2020. This is how we recommend getting there independently: 1. Overnight bus from El Chaltén to Los Antiguos: Those travelling Patagonia on a shorter itinerary will usually visit El Chaltén. A magnificent playground for outdoor enthusiasts. For those able to travel Patagonia longer, El Chaltén is a great launch pad for the long journey north to Puerto Rio Tranquilo for the Marble Caves. Never ideal, the overnight bus is a time efficient way to cover the distance. As far as we’re aware, there are no other real options. Like all buses in Patagonia, we felt completely safe. The bus departs 9pm, arriving in Los Antiguos 7:30-8am. We paid $49USD/person for a one way ticket online. Tickets can also be purchased in the main bus terminal. If booking this way, we would recommend doing so at least a few days ahead of time just in case Please note that for the rest of the journey, it is well known, that booking and planning in advance can be very difficult. Verging on near impossible. Therefore, flexibility with your itinerary is still required. 2. Bus from Los Antiguos (Argentina) crossing the border to Chile Chico (Chile) What we didn’t know was that Chaltén Travel run a morning bus service from Los Antiguos to Chile Chico. This leaves at 8:30am for around $15USD/person. This is perfect, as your overnight bus from El Chaltén will arrive at Los Antiguos in time! Even with this knowledge, we could not find the route to book anywhere online. However, it is possible to book this ticket at the Chaltén Travel office, in the El Chaltén bus station. Hence we would HIGHLY recommend booking the Los Antiguos to Chile Chico bus ticket upon arrival in El Chaltén. You should book this along with the overnight bus if you hadn’t done so already on. Please note that we tried to book the Los Antiguos to Chile Chico bus ticket the night of boarding the overnight bus in El Chaltén. It was sold out. The above information is critical in order to plan your route to the Marble Caves. Not knowing this meant we had to cross the border between Los Antiguos and Chile Chico on foot! This was an adventure in its own right and didn’t cost a thing. But it meant arriving into Chile Chico around 11:45am. This was too late for the bus services to Puerto Rio Tranquilo. They only run in the morning. Specifically, the bus from Los Antiguos should arrive in Chile Chico around 9:30-10am. This would be in time for the buses that head to Puerto Rio Tranquilo! What if you miss the Chile Chico to Puerto Rio Tranquilo bus? Don't worry! It happened to us. Because of this, we had an unexpected night in Chile Chico. We had to wait until the next day for the bus to Puerto Rio Tranquilo. It was annoying as we were so excited to get to the Marble Caves and didn't want to be wasting anytime. But at least it gave us a day to relax. Admittedly, Chile Chico doesn't get much tourism except for those passing by on their way north. So accommodation was plentiful. We cannot remember where we stayed, but we had the whole hotel to ourselves. We even got to pick the room we wanted! Plus, there's always a chance that something like this can happen when travelling a rural area with irregular transport. 3. Bus from Chile Chico to Puerto Rio Tranquilo All buses going from Chile Chico to Puerto Rio Tranquilo are privately owned mini van transportation. They are all found at the main bus station in Chile Chico. As far as we’re aware, these companies do not display any bus departure times or confirmed days of travel online. Call or email them directly. That's your best chance for up to date information As of March 2020, these were the 2 private mini van companies doing the daily route. They both charge $15,000CLP ($18USD) Unfortunately, according to Turismo Tramal, their current departure time, as of 21 March 2020, is 9am. As the bus from Los Antiguos does not arrive until approximately an hour later, you would be unable to take this bus if you wanted to leave for Puerto Rio Tranquilo the same day. However, when we visited in February 2020, there was definitely a bus departing at 11:30am with this company. Therefore, when it’s your turn getting to the Marble Caves in Patagonia, make sure to contact the company to find out the latest. Fortunately, Transportes Costa Carrera has a 10am departure and can be reserved in advance. Now you might be thinking, will my bus from Los Antiguos make it in time? The good news is, Transportes Costa Carrera actually works with Chaltén Travel and wait until the Los Antiguos bus arrives before departing to Puerto Rio Tranquilo. In the worst case scenario that you miss the morning bus in Chile Chico, Transportes Costa Carrera may offer another option. They offered us a transport service to Puerto Rio Tranquilo for around $130,000CLP ($155USD) split between a maximum of 4 people ($32,500CLP/$38.50USD per person). This was if we could find others interested. We decided against this because the normal bus service is much cheaper. But it can be a last resort option. Apparently, several companies in town can arrange this. But we had significant difficulty locating them. We hope this helps, Dan & Beck from Travel Made Me Do It

review_text: During our visit to Santiago, we stayed at the Santiago Marriott in the newer los Condes area of Santiago, east of the old town. It is a beautiful up-and-coming part of the city full of tree-lined streets and striking tall modern buildings. Its central feature is a long stretch of greenspace known as Parque Araucano. This is one of the most lovely inviting urban parks we have ever had the pleasure to enjoy anywhere. It must be 2-3 kilometers long from east to west, and perhaps half a kilometer wide full of broad, well-maintained reach of turf, and thousands of verdant trees offering welcome shade over the hard-packed sand paths for strollers like us, joggers and dog walkers. It features immaculate play fields, fountains, a small aviary, and a skateboard park. There is also a sparkling set of buildings, apparently a sort of science center for kids which we did not enter, although we were attracted by the surprising presence of the forward part of a LAN airliner protruding from one of the buildings. The park is a perfect centerpiece and binding element for the entire modern neighborhood of high-rise offices and apartments, and one which would certainly attract us to live and work in the area if we were lucky to have this in our own country. Well done Santiago!

There is also a sparkling set of buildings, apparently a sort of science center for kids which we did not enter, although we were attracted by the surprising presence of the forward part of a LAN airliner protruding from one of the buildings. The park is a perfect centerpiece and binding element for the entire modern neighborhood of high-rise offices and apartments, and one which would certainly attract us to live and work in the area if we were lucky to have this in our own country. Well done Santiago!

review_text: We were on a solar eclipse tour with limited time in San Pedro so booked this tour specifically to get a custom itinerary and some great photo opportunities. Patrice and his father really delivered. Not only were they very helpful and flexible with a late date change but we had the best possible day. They started by serving us a delicious breakfast overlooking Laguna Tuyajto at over 4000m and sub zero with an infusion tea that quickly counteracted the altitude lightheadedness. After a few photos it was back to Salar de Águas Calientes and a distant viuew of the closed Piedras Rojas. Then on to Lagunas Miscanti and Miñiques for yet more stunning views and photos. In passing we photograhed Vicuna, cute viscachas ansd a desert fox before reacjing Socaire and its charning church. Then across the Salar de Ayacama to Laguna Chaxa where there were a few Flamingos in the midst of the stunning salt flats. After that it was time for a late lunch served up in the El Tambillo forest plantation. Patrice the elder certainly put his 25 years as a trucker to good use rustling up delightfully tasty roast chicken with salad and bread plus wine or soft drinks followed by dessert under the shady trees, while a herd of goats went by, with the mountains as a stunning backdrop. Patrice the younger is incredibly knowlegable about the Atacama environment and really passionate about preserving it against the threats of global warming and exploitation. After lunch it was off to the Valley of the Moon until sunset. I think that was about as much as could be fitted into one day, You would need 3 conventional tours to do so much without the same enjoyment and background knowledge. Review of: Lagunas Altiplanicas fullday private
