review_text: We contacted Elki Magic about three months before our visit to Vicuna and Adeline responded the same day with information of all their tours. She also sent lots of other helpful information before we finally arrived, including updates on what the Chilean people referred to as "The Situation" which had developed just after our arrival in Santiago. We found the EM office easily and by the end of our bike journey the following day we had met all the family - Adeline, Lincoln, their two lovely children as well as Adeline's father who was visiting from France - and been given lots of inside info. about the area and facilities. SO, what about the bike tour which we booked with them? It was nothing short of fantastic!! We followed the route on the EM map (about 18 km) and visited many of the suggested sites, including the ABA pisco distillery (we had to be abstemious as we had to re-mount the bikes to continue!), Eco Truly (the local Hare Krishna community where we were given lovely cool water and were even invited to lunch) and, just after the halfway point, the Guayacan Brewery where we tasted six different brews - just the job to cool down in the shade as it was a swelteringly hot day. We even got a discount for being on the EM route, which was even better!! We also got a discount for lunch at the Solar Restaurant "Delicias del Sol" - definitely misnamed, but we won't go into detail as this was the lowlight of our adventure. When we returned to the office other people were returning their bikes after doing different tours and they all seemed delighted with their experiences. We would definitely recommend Elki Magic to anyone visiting the Elqui Valley whether they want to do one of the bike rides or any of the other tours.

review_text: The trip around Cape Horn was part of 4 weeks spent in South America (you can read about some of the rest of it with my other reviews). Having inherited some money from an uncle I decided that the best thing I could do would be to do some travelling because he never got the chance to do so. So I organised a four week trip around Peru, Chile, and Brazil! Along with Rio de Janeiro, this trip to Cape Horn was one of the highlights of the trip (that and Machu Picchu of course!). While many others have sailed around the Cape, few have actually landed on it, and like other reviewers here I was on the Stella Australis from Punta Arenas, Chile to Ushuaia, Argentina. A couple of people I spoke to before I went said they had friends or relatives that had been to Cape Horn and that it was no big deal, but as it turned out they had been on big cruise ships and had only been past it! Fingers crossed that we would be able to stop and land when we got there because the weather is notorious for being changeable even during 'high' summer which is when I was there, a couple of days after Christmas 2011. We were lucky because the sea was quite 'calm', and we were able to land and walk about the Cape itself. It started to rain, but what the heck, none of us cared! How many people have a picture of themselves (taken by someone else!) standing in front of the Cape Horn monument? The feeling must be about the same as if you had just climbed Everest! The Cape itself is bleak (I was reminded a bit of the Shetlands at the top of the world), facilities are almost existent but there is a delightful little church. It was enough to just be there! And the cruise itself? Well TA don't seem to think we want to review cruise ships but a few words about the Stella Australis will not be out of place. Beautiful ship, I was travelling alone but as the cruise was not full I had a lovely twin cabin to myself. As you would expect the crew are wonderful, the lecturers are informative without being too technical and they are honest enough to admit that mistakes were made with the indigenous population a long time ago. And the Stella Australis has been especially designed for these waters so it can go places that the big cruise ships cannot, a great trip for nautre buffs and birdwatchers. Cruising past the glaciers with food and alcohol to suit each 'nationality' is a great idea although the rest of the evening was a bit hazy. Any particular gripe about the MV Stella Australis? Yes of course, very difficult to get a table for one in the dining room, and the main courses are all a bit the same, and eating was a bit difficult when the menu has seafood for starters and fish for main course when you allergic to both. Of course the waiters came to the rescue and gave me the children's menu....... You just have to visit Cape Horn as part of a trip to South America. This cruise is not for those with dodgy knees and hips, there is quite a lot of walking around on rough paths but when you get to land on Cape Horn there is a good staircase going up and you can take your time, and there are good raised walkways.

review_text: Magdalena island is a bit off the main land. It is accessed by Zodiac boat. The trip is worth it with the caution that some agility is needed. While there are attendants, a visitor must climb out of the boat on narrow iron steps. Once on shore, there are sidewalks to guide your visit. People are asked to stay on the paths as the island is a breeding ground for penguins. There are hundreds of penguins and their little bungalow nests are everywhere. Seagulls are also abundant, waiting for a chick to snatch. This is a natural preserve and the birds have no fear of humans. Visitors are asked to give them the right-of-way, as they might be sharing or crossing the paths. The entire route is about a mile and the visit might take an hour or less.

review_text: Having been to the top of the Burj in Dubai, the Empire State Building and the Sears Tower, as well as the Menara in Kuala Lumpur (and missing a chance at the World Trade Center in the 90s), I figured this was a box I needed to check, though with the CLP10K adult admission cost (about US$15) it seemed that a lot hinged on the tallest-in-Latin-America bragging right. My time was also hemmed in, so I couldn't time it for a great-weather day. Though maybe it's just as well, as I can imagine much bigger crowds on such types of days, especially around sunset. In my case there were clouds limiting visibility and of course smog, but maybe that's closer to the "real" Santiago and there was enough viewing distance to see some of the Andes (still towering higher than this building) and also get an appreciation for how many people must live in Santiago, what with the sea of apartment buildings. Didn't take the tour, darn the luck. But on a mediocre day like the one where I went, you could sit down and linger and ponder without hassle, and that was worth something (especially to introverts). Again, probably much different and more people on the nicer days, especially if on weekends. The building and its shopping center aren't next to a metro stop, but the walk to Tobalba station is only 5 minutes or so. The mall underneath is large enough to have echoes of Parque Arauco and as potential redoubt for the just-won't-adapt gringo crowd (for whom the Hard Rock Cafe is the big dining adventure and Applebee's the "safe" choice).

review_text: This museum was at the top of my list of places to see in Santiago. I studied the Pinochet years a great deal in school and was interested to learn more from a Chilean perspective. I personally loved the experience but would note a couple of things for those thinking about going there: 1) It's free!! Which means it is a great way to learn a little bit of history for those on a budget. 2) The idea for the museum was founded by a torture victim from the Pinochet era, so it is telling one side of the story only. It is a story about human rights violations, not about politics, so don't go there expecting to learn a great deal about the political background before, during or after Pinochet's reign. I disagree with the comments that it is propaganda, but it is a one-sided story. 3) Very little English, so if you do not understand Spanish, you probably won't get as much out of the experience. 4) It is not a light-hearted experience. This focuses on a very dark period in history. Considering these things, I personally had a great experience. Reading about events in a textbook cannot compare to seeing the pictures and videos of victims laid out before you in such a personalized manor.

review_text: The Bolivian Winter phenomenon creates a microclimate in San Pedro vallley, and so the tours were moved to the fierce heat of the late morning. Being an Englishwoman this was no deterrent, so I trekked up the ridge for the amazing views. The nearby Vallley of Mars is also reallly interesting and my tour finished by driving us to a panorama over the whole area. So despite missing the sunset and the stars I was able to appreciate this amazing landscape. However maybe the likelihood of cloudy conditions and mudslides causing disruption to schedules should be better advertised. And how about having a beautiful museum for everyone to enjoy when there are poor weather conditions or if you have children who could get a fun experience seeing star panoramas in a cool safe location when they are awake? The precolombian museum in Santiago has a temporary exhibition that is of a high standard, so it is disappointing there is nothing in Atacama. review_text: Even in the rain, this was a very enjoyable day along the beautiful coast. I was actually a little surprised, how fascinating the late poet Pablo Neruba's home was. The tour through the house is very well done and easy to follow. You are given headsets in your own language that explain Neruda's lifestyle and home. We also had a nice lunch at a local restaurant in the town of Pomaire which is also known for their pottery. The food was delicious, but be warned, the portions are huge. Probably can share a meal. We also really enjoyed our visit at the beautiful Undurraga Vineyard. Daniel was a wonderful guide who was very friendly, knowledgable and fun. He made the day extra special. He also went above and beyond to help us out with a situation that was not related to the tour. In conversation, we casually mentioned the issue we were having locating my lost laptop at the airport. review_text: Did one-week expedition to Chilean Andes mountains with Allmountian over the new Year break. We've climbed two prominent peaks over Santiago, Cerro Leonera (4954 m), and Cerro El Plomo (5434 m). Love every moment of it! The guides I went with, Balthasar and Charlie, are both very experienced mountaineers, spending a lot of time in the mountains and doing ascents on numerous Andean peaks between 6000 and 7000 meters. They are guiding both technical and non technical routes, and actually way many more different mountains than I can see on the website. Also, so great people to go with, nice, caring, well educated, protective for the environment. Charming and greatly spirited atmosphere, super delicious hot meal tree times a day (so much better than lyophilized food I've used to use...). Plus many interesting and enjoyable conversations, a lot of cultural exchange. Both guides are fluent in English, and eagerly taught me some Spanish whenever I've asked. Transportation of packs on the mules to the base camp also helps a lot. Altogether it lead to summiting both peaks successfully, and it was incredibly enjoyable experience. This was my first trip to high Andes, and the beauty of the mountains blended with meditative and authentic Andean music that I've selected to listen at the base camp from the big music collection will stay in my heart. The vacation is short, but I will definitely go again with you guys! Nadiya! Thank you very much for your comment and for trusting us to make this beautiful expedition in the Andes Mountains. We enjoyed a lot, the music, the conversations in the dome, and the sharing with you every day, it was undoubtedly an unforgettable expedition. We hope you come back to Chile so we can share again a nice adventure in the mountains together. A big hug from the entire Allmountain Chile team.

review_text: This was our favorite attraction in Valparaiso and one of our favorites during our trip to Chile. The Museo de Historia Natural de Valparaiso is a small, but free museum with interesting exhibits in a beautiful, old building. Very few of the displays feature English signage, although it's possible to understand everything if you have a passable ability to read Spanish. There were lots of kids in the museum on the day we visited and it's definitely a site that would appeal to children, even if they don't read/understand Spanish. The exhibit on deep-sea creatures is particularly interesting. We learned a lot about the natural history of the area and appreciated that the museum had a strong environmentalist/conservation message. We took TAer's recommendations and had coffee in the small cafe at the entrance. It was by far the best coffee we had in Chile.
